oracle_gaps: Check#check_lead (lead-span grammar) and Check#check_temporal_time are excluded here: their grammars are campaign 5. This slice must not claim their tests.

`Check` discards every reason `Recur` produced. `Recur.parse_result` returns richly specific rejections (`day of month must be 1–31: "32"`, `unknown day of week: "xyz"`, why `.+` cannot prefix a calendar schedule); `check_task` calls the boolean `Recur.cookie?` instead, so all twenty-seven rows of `malformed/recur-non-canonical` collapse into one message that varies only by the inspected value. On the `check` surface a port therefore owes `cookie?` fidelity ONLY — accept/reject agreement and the one fixed message. Wiring the richer per-reason diagnostics into `check` would be more helpful to a user and would still be a divergence. Those messages ARE user-visible on the input surface (`tasks recur`, `Recur.explain`), which is a different slice: one grammar, validated twice, at two levels of diagnosis.

`Recur.cookie?` and `Check` disagree on whitespace-padded values: ' w:mon' and 'w:mon ' are true to `cookie?` (it strips) and rejected by `check_task`'s `rc == rc.strip` guard. `malformed/recur-non-canonical` carries both rows. A port that validates recurrence by calling its own parser and nothing else accepts them and passes every other row in the file. The same fixture's middle group is the other trap: eleven values that PARSE but are not canonical (`1w:mon`, `w:monday`, `w:wed,mon`, `m:01`, `m:15,1`, `y:7-04`, …) are refused because `Recur.schedule` accepts a stored string only when `canonical_calendar` reproduces it exactly — day-of-month is not zero-padded, the yearly month is.

td-794997 (FIXTURES-2, 2026-08-01) — RESOLVED IN RUBY, not in the prose. This slice's behavior sentence and `Links.extract`'s comment both said the labelled form survives a dedupe; the implementation sorted by offset and `uniq(&:url)`, so the EARLIEST occurrence won and a label survived only when it happened to appear first. `valid/link-corpus` carries the same url in both orders — 11c00009 labelled-first, 11c00010 bare-first — which is how the divergence was caught, and an implementation written from either written spec passed the first and failed the second. Marcus decided the BEHAVIOR was wrong rather than the prose: `Links.extract` now folds occurrences into an insertion-ordered map keyed by url, so the first LABELLED occurrence wins outright and a bare one stands in only when no occurrence is labelled. Order is unchanged — a later label replaces an earlier bare entry in place, so every surviving link still sits at its url's first occurrence. The fixture README was re-recorded from the new oracle (11c00010 gains `(Later label)`; 11c00009 is byte-identical and is the control). A PORT MUST NOT implement `uniq`-by-first-occurrence: that is the pre-fix oracle and the corpus no longer describes it. One rule is pinned by unit test only — when one url carries TWO DIFFERENT labels the first labelled occurrence wins outright and labels never merge — because no corpus record spells the same url with two distinct labels.

Tasks::Atomic IS directly tested — test/test_journal.rb holds eight cases covering the temp sibling, the inode-swapping rename, permission carry-over, symlink and dangling-symlink following, and a chmod-refusing filesystem — and they are claimed above. Sidecar names follow the symlink, by two independent code paths that must agree. td-d6ed92 (FIXTURES-3, 2026-08-01): `ensure_id!` is a RECORD repair, not a store repair, and a store with two or more id-less records cannot be repaired by any command. `with_history` has no preflight, so `malformed/missing-ids-many` mints one id and the post-write `Check` over the whole file still fails, rolling the write back (`file failed validation after the edit`, exit 1) — whereas `tasks capture` on the same store refuses BEFORE writing (`task file is already invalid … (nothing was written)`). `ensure_id!` remains a RECORD repair with no preflight, and converges only when its record is the file's last remaining error: on a store with two or more id-less records it mints one, fails the post-write Check on the rest, and rolls back with `file failed validation after the edit` (td-d6ed92). `Store#repair!` is the separate store-wide minter that converges n>=2, drawing ids from one pool spanning live and archive so it cannot invent the cross-file duplicate `check --all-files` refuses. The two refusal wordings stay distinct and are contract: a preflight refusal says `task file is already invalid ... (nothing was written)`, a rolled-back write says `file failed validation after the edit`. Adding a preflight to `ensure_id!` looks like a harmless optimization and would silently emit the wrong one.

behavior: Three-way record merge, field level: non-overlapping fields union, same-field conflicts resolved last-writer-wins on `updated` and commutatively, temporal date/time pairs resolved as one value, tags unioned, body prefix-append, state progression, and the schema-version refusals on all three sides

The merge's version rule is NOT the store's: `allow_older` is true for the base and false for both sides, so a base at an older version still merges while a side at any version other than Format::VERSION refuses. A port that reuses `Store#unsupported_schema?` here would refuse merges git can currently resolve. This asymmetry has no counterpart anywhere else in the codebase and is the single most likely misport in the slice.

`updated` and `line` are excluded from the merge (EXCLUDED_FIELDS) but `updated` is also the tiebreaker — the field the merge reads and never writes. Nothing in the suite asserts what the merged record's own `updated` value ends up as, because the driver leaves it to the next write. Characterization must pin it before translating.

Merge decisions are logged as events and the log text is written to `.tasks-merge.log` by the driver, so `format_event`'s wording is observable to users. No test asserts the exact wording of more than a few events; merge-driver-git claims the log-shape test and this slice must capture the event vocabulary it produces.

Schema-v1 migration and org-mode are out of scope (Marcus, 2026-08-01, no schema-v1 users exist) and td-09f7de removed them from Ruby, so this slice's oracle no longer carries them: there is no `tasks migrate`, no `migrate_schema!`, and no `migration_required` status. What remains IS contract and must be ported: any declared `meta` version other than 2 is refused identically, older or newer — `Check` reports `unsupported meta version <n> (expected 2)`, `Store#unsupported_schema?` gates mutations on both files, refusals carry the `:unsupported_schema` status and write nothing, and the API answers `503 unsupported_schema_version`. Omitting that gate is a data-corruption bug, not a skipped dead branch. Org-mode remains out of scope entirely.

A PORT MUST NOT QUOTE `%L`/`%X`/`%Y` in the configured driver command string. Git pre-quotes those labels in the sequencer path — rebase and cherry-pick pass `'a1b2c3 (ours)'` already quoted — so wrapping them again produces `''a1b2c3 (ours)''`, a shell syntax error. The driver then never runs at all and git silently falls back to its own line-based text merge on tasks.jsonl, which is the exact outcome this driver exists to prevent. The failure is invisible to `git merge`, which passes either way: it is only reachable by driving rebase or cherry-pick, which is why both are now in the oracle. All three arguments are optional (arity 4..7) so installs carrying the older four-argument string keep working, falling back to marker width 7 and the labels ours/theirs.
fixtures_todo: Needs a git-shaped fixture rather than a store-shaped one: a repo with .gitattributes registering tasks.jsonl and archive.jsonl, two branches that diverge on one line of tasks.jsonl, and the expected post-merge file. The existing corpus has no git repositories at all, and the fixture contract (a directory containing store/) does not describe one, so this needs a new fixture class or an explicit decision that the merge cases are built by the runner instead. That decision is worth taking before building anything: a committed git repo inside a git repo is awkward, and a runner that runs `git init` and two commits is deterministic enough for conformance.

notes: This is the capability users install into their own repos, so its failure mode is other people's data. The contract with git is that a non-zero exit leaves the conflict for the human — and because git copies %A back over the working file on failure exactly as on success, "leaves the conflict" means the driver must WRITE it: on every refusal it fences ours and theirs verbatim between `<<<<<<<` / `=======` / `>>>>>>>` with the reason on the opening marker. That both sides survive byte-for-byte, and that `tasks check` then rejects the file, is the single most important assertion in the slice; a refusal that wrote nothing would leave a clean, markerless, check-passing tasks.jsonl holding only ours, which `git add` stages by reflex and which discards the whole other side (td-7b9c01).

`command_on_path?`'s EXPLICIT-PATH BRANCH IS UNTESTED, and it is the mechanism four fixtures_todo in this campaign rest on (review finding 6, porting/evidence/wiring/campaign-10-review.md). `available?` returns `File.executable?(bin)` directly whenever the command contains a `/`, and searches PATH otherwise; all three availability tests in the suite pass a BARE name (`definitely-not-a-real-binary-xyz`, `ruby`, and Hermes' probe). A port that implements the method as PATH-search-only passes every one of them — and then no `<provider>_command = ./fake-harness` config can ever make a harness available, which silently disables the entire fake-harness corpus this campaign's conformance story depends on. Characterize the branch before translating: an absolute path, a relative path, a path to a non-executable file, and a path to a directory.

Cancellation is timing-dependent by construction: #test_async_agent_cancellation_escalates_when_child_ignores_term asserts that a TERM-ignoring child is killed in under one wall-clock second, against CANCEL_TERM_GRACE + CANCEL_KILL_GRACE = 0.30s of budget. That is a latency assertion, and no determinism pin in porting/specs/determinism.md can pin it. Two implementations can both be correct and disagree on elapsed time; a conformance comparison of this behavior would have to compare the OUTCOME (process_status.signaled?, termsig == KILL) and explicitly exclude timing, which the current observation schema cannot express because it records neither.

`Process.wait2`, `Process.kill(sig, -pid)`, `pgroup: true` and `Process.detach` are POSIX process-group operations. Windows has no equivalent of signalling a negative pid, so the escalation ladder is not portable as written and this slice is platform-scoped rather than `any`. Nothing in the suite runs on Windows, so there is no oracle for what the behavior there should even be — that is a design decision for the port, not a test to translate.

Three branches have no test at all: the `rescue StandardError` in #start that closes both pipe ends and re-raises when spawn fails (an unreadable binary), the `Errno::ECHILD` paths in #finish and #reap_within (a child reaped by something else), and #detach_unreaped_child (a child that survives KILL, i.e. uninterruptible sleep). All three are reachable in production and all three must be characterized by hand before translating.

The 65_536-byte read chunk and the `force_encoding("UTF-8")` on it are load-bearing and untested: a multi-byte character split across two chunk boundaries is the realistic failure, and no test feeds the pump a UTF-8 transcript larger than one chunk. test/test_agent_activity.rb#test_wraps_unicode_prompt_and_transcript_to_requested_width proves the renderer scrubs, not that the pump preserves.

Two details the first draft of this todo got wrong, both caught by the review (findings 7 and 9) and both fatal to a corpus built from it. FIRST, the exit control cannot be a normal argv scan: `cmd_prompt` does `prompt = words.join(" ")` and every adapter passes the result as ONE argv element (for Cursor and Hermes it is buried further, inside the element that also carries the prepended system context), so `-p "--exit 3"` hands the harness a single argument `"--exit 3"` and a token scan finds nothing. The script must search each argv element for an embedded `--exit N` substring. SECOND, the reason a relative `./fake-harness` works is NOT that the harness is chdir'd there: `available?` calls `File.executable?` in the `tasks` process, against THAT process's cwd, and the `chdir:` on the spawn is not in play for the check at all. It works because two independent things coincide — the runner's case `cwd` defaults to `"."`, which is the copy root, and `cp -a <fixture>/store/. <copy>/` lands tasks.jsonl at the copy root so `data_dir = File.dirname(ORG)` is the same directory. Therefore: CASES AGAINST THIS FIXTURE MUST NOT SET `cwd`. The protocol permits it, and a case that sets it to a subdirectory breaks `available?` while leaving the spawn workable — and the failure presents as `the agent isn't available`, indistinguishable from the no-fixture baseline. No case needs to set PATH, which the protocol forbids. The fixture makes the spawn, the argv, the working directory and the exit status observable as file bytes in `files.after`. It does NOT make cancellation observable: nothing in the protocol can send a signal mid-run.

`--dangerously-skip-permissions` (Claude), `--force` (Cursor) and `--yolo --accept-hooks` (Hermes) are the flags that let an autonomous harness edit files without a prompt. They are asserted as literal strings and nothing proves the consequence — that the harness actually runs unattended. A port that reproduces the argv exactly is doing all this slice can prove; verifying the flags still mean that is an operational check on every harness upgrade.

Hermes' `stream:` split is the only place the flag changes the command, and the reason is recorded only in comments: `chat -q` streams a transcript including tool previews (the TUI wants it) while `-z/--oneshot` prints only the final answer (the sync CLI wants it). A port that made Claude branch on `stream:` would pass this list.

Both need a stub HTTP server to characterize, which the suite does not have.

Hermes' `available?` performs a real HTTP request to a configured URL. Under the runner protocol the invocation environment is constructed and pinned but the network is not, so a conformance case that reached this code path would be observing the operator's machine. Any case for Hermes must point ollama_url at a closed port through the fixture's config file and assert the unavailable branch only; the available branch is not conformance-testable without a network fake the protocol has no way to declare.

oracle_gaps: config-resolution's single oracle_gap says the unclaimed remainder of test/test_config.rb — prompt-facts among them — `belong to campaign 8's CLI and TUI work`. That sentence was written before campaign 10 existed and is now wrong for the seven prompt-facts tests specifically: they configure what an agent sees, not how a human reads output. This slice claims them, and config-resolution's sentence has been corrected in the same pass to say so. The host-context keys in that same file remain unclaimed and remain campaign 8's / create-basic's, exactly as before.

The `prompt.<name>` config parsing lives in lib/tasks/config.rb, which config-resolution also names in its source_paths for the path rules. Both slices list the file and neither ports all of it: config-resolution owns store-path resolution, this slice owns the `prompt.<name>` key parse — `PromptFacts::FACT_NAME` matching, `parse_toggle` accepting on/true/1 and off/false/0, a bare `prompt.` key ignored. The overlap is deliberate rather than a double claim: the file is named twice, no test is, and it has to be named here because prompt_facts.rb is required BY config.rb and not the reverse, so a prompt-facts-only closure would not watch the parse rule for drift at all.

Both registered providers are environment reads: `Time.now` and `Socket.gethostname`. The tests inject both through the `clock:`/`hostname:` lambdas, which is the only reason this slice has a clean oracle. Production has no injection — it calls them directly — and the runner protocol pins `TASKS_PIN_NOW` and `TASKS_PIN_HOSTNAME`, so a conformance case CAN observe the rendered block deterministically, but only if the port routes both facts through the same pins. A port that reads the OS clock here while honoring the pin everywhere else produces a system prompt that differs on every run and a conformance failure that looks like flake.

#test_format_datetime_is_agent_friendly pins the strftime `%Y-%m-%d %a %H:%M %Z`, which includes a ZONE ABBREVIATION. Abbreviations are tzdb data, not format, and porting/specs/observations.schema.json records `environment.tzdb_version` precisely because two hosts can disagree. Under the pinned `TZ=UTC`/`TASKS_TIMEZONE=UTC` environment this renders `UTC` on any host, so it is safe for conformance — but only under that pin.

The registry is explicitly designed to grow (`a flaky future source (weather, ...)`) and the silent-omission rule exists for that growth. Nothing tests a provider that is slow rather than failing; there is no timeout on `safe_value`, so a future blocking provider would hang every agent run. That is a latent defect in Ruby, not a porting note, and is recorded here because this is where a port would faithfully reproduce it.

oracle_gaps: THIS IS A PROMPT-INJECTION BOUNDARY, and the oracle proves the fence rather than its sufficiency. agent-memory.md is untrusted content — it can arrive by `git pull` or `git clone` — and the only defense is that a body containing MEMORY_BEGIN or MEMORY_END is a hard error (#test_memory_containing_a_delimiter_line_raises). Nothing tests a body that ends the fence by other means, and nothing can: whether a model honours a delimiter is not a property of this code. A port must reproduce the check exactly — including that it is a REFUSAL and never a sanitize-and-continue — and reviewers should treat weakening it as a security regression, not a formatting choice.

`Tasks::Config::Paths#agent_context` — the `File locations for this run` heredoc naming the CLI, tasks.jsonl, archive.jsonl and agent-memory.md as absolute paths — physically lives in lib/tasks/config.rb, which config-resolution ports for its path-resolution rules. This slice owns the block's content and ordering (proved by #test_includes_agents_contract_and_absolute_paths) and reaches the file through the require closure, so drift on config.rb fires for both slices. No test is shared between them.

The section order (contract, environment, locations, pointer, memory) is asserted only pairwise: #test_includes_current_environment_before_file_locations pins one adjacency. Nothing asserts the full five-section order or the two-newline join, and a port that emitted the memory block before the file locations would pass every test here while handing the agent its user defaults before it knows where anything is.

TASK_AGENT.md is read from the APPLICATION CHECKOUT (`cli_root`), not the data directory, and its absence is tolerated (#test_missing_contract_file_still_builds_from_paths_and_pointer). oracle_gaps: THE TWO REFUSAL WORDINGS ARE THE POINT OF THIS SLICE AND ARE EASY TO COLLAPSE. A preflight refusal says `task file is already invalid — run `tasks check` (nothing was written)`; a write that was rolled back says `file failed validation after the edit`. td-d6ed92 records that adding a preflight to `ensure_id!` looks like a harmless optimization and would silently emit the wrong one. `repair` exists BESIDE those paths and changes neither: on a store with two or more id-less records `tasks id` still writes, still fails the post-write Check and still rolls back. The `updated` stamp is deliberately NOT written on a repair (`write_records(..., stamp: false)`), and a port that stamps will pass every single-device case and corrupt multi-device merges: `updated` is the last-write-wins tiebreaker, so a repairing device that stamps beats the peer which UNDERSTOOD a dropped unknown temporal key with the copy that just discarded it. No conformance case can observe this, because the corpus is single-device; it is proved only by #test_repair_leaves_the_updated_stamp_exactly_as_it_found_it.

Minting is deliberately narrow and the asymmetry is load-bearing: an ABSENT id is minted, a MALFORMED one is left alone and refuses. Children may point at a malformed id and reminting would orphan them, whereas an absent id can never be a parent because Check resolves `parent` only against ids it has seen. A port that repairs both looks more helpful and silently reparents tasks.

The WIDE and ZERO_WIDTH tables in `lib/char_width.rb` are HAND-MAINTAINED codepoint range lists, not a generated Unicode property export, and the suite samples them at about a dozen codepoints. A Go port that reaches for a rune-width library instead of transcribing the tables will disagree with Ruby at some codepoint no test names — most likely a text-presentation symbol, which this file deliberately keeps at ONE cell (the comment names the warning sign U+26A0 and the check mark U+2713) where several width libraries say two. The tables ARE the contract. Port them literally, and keep them in one place, which is the entire reason `char_width.rb` exists: `Tui::Ansi` and `TermForm::Text` each carried a verbatim copy and one perf regression lived in both.

Grapheme segmentation is Ruby's `each_grapheme_cluster`, i.e. whatever Unicode version Ruby was built against; Go's segmentation comes from a different library at a possibly different version. `test_wrap_never_splits_grapheme_clusters` and `test_vtrunc_does_not_split_wide_char` prove the RULE, not the table, and nothing in the suite or the schema pins the Unicode version on either side. Same class as determinism.md's `environment.tzdb_version` note: recorded, never compared, and a human re-runs before classifying a mismatch.

The fast path in `CharWidth.char_width` (printable ASCII returns before the ~75 linear `cover?` scans) is a deliberate perf decision whose comment says the scans otherwise dominated modal compositing and field rendering. No test asserts it and no perf gate exists to hold it, so a port that drops it is invisible to the whole suite. `perf_budget` is null because there is nothing in the tree to check it against, not because the cost is imaginary.

`Ansi.wrap` scrubs invalid UTF-8 and accepts ASCII-8BIT input (`test_wrap_handles_binary_encoded_utf8`, `test_wrap_scrubs_invalid_utf8`, `test_vtrunc_binary_wrapped_line_roundtrip`, `test_cell_slice_normalizes_invalid_binary_utf8`) — Ruby encoding-tag behavior with no Go analogue, since a Go string is bytes with no tag. The behavior to preserve is the one the tests actually assert: invalid bytes never raise and never change the visible width. The port must decide what its equivalent input is and say so.

The behavior to preserve is that a later resize cannot retroactively move an already-open modal — the layout is sampled once and copied — and the port must prove it by mutating the source after sampling and asserting the placement did not move, not by asking whether a value is frozen.

The breakpoint tests are EXACT-boundary characterizations rather than samples: `test_panel_content_widths_characterize_editor_breakpoint_boundaries`, `test_editing_admission_is_exact_at_minimum_terminal_width`, `test_editing_admission_is_exact_at_named_height_across_widths_and_modes` and `test_each_footer_row_raises_edit_height_minimum` assert that admission flips between adjacent integer sizes. EVERY ASSERTION HERE IS OVER THE FRAME'S LINE ARRAY, an internal Ruby abstraction the observation schema has no name for (inventory §5d), and there is no golden-screen corpus anywhere in this repository. Nothing in this slice is proved against captured terminal output; it is proved against the string list `Tui::Frame` returns. The port therefore has to reproduce the ABSTRACTION and not merely the visible result — a Go implementation that paints correctly through a different intermediate type cannot run these tests at all. That is a real constraint on the port's shape, and it is stated here rather than discovered halfway through translation.

The overlay tests deliberately probe hostile geometry — negative left edge, popups and modals wider than the frame, minimum terminal size, and wide clusters straddling the splice point (`test_popup_clips_cleanly_at_negative_left_edge`, `test_wide_popup_is_clipped_without_overflow_at_right_edge`, `test_popup_splices_at_terminal_cell_boundaries`, `test_popup_preserves_styles_around_wide_base_content`, `test_mixed_unicode_frames_respect_narrow_width_boundaries`). These are the tests most likely to pass in Ruby and fail in Go for a reason belonging to `tui-text-metrics` rather than to this slice: the splice is done in CELLS, and a port that splices in bytes or in runes is green on ASCII and corrupts every row carrying an emoji badge.

`test_hit_map_list_cells_match_rendered_row_glyphs` is claimed HERE rather than by `tui-hit-map` because the assertion is over the rendered frame, and it is the single test tying painted cells to click zones. `tui-hit-map` carries a dep edge on this slice for that reason. A port that keeps paint and hit test in sync BY CONSTRUCTION (one span computation feeding both) is materially better than one that keeps them in sync by test, and the Ruby already does the former.

Truecolor capability is unpinned — see `tui-theme-and-border`'s gap. It is recorded twice on purpose: the gap lives in the theme slice, the visible damage lands here, in `test_frame_chrome_carries_gradient_under_truecolor`.

Scroll behavior is proved at the boundary only by `test_scrolls_to_keep_selection_visible`. Nothing proves what happens when the selection is beyond the row list, when the viewport is taller than the content, or when a resize shrinks the viewport under a selection that was visible. The right-panel half is better served (`test_replacing_same_identity_preserves_scroll`, `test_replacing_new_identity_resets_scroll`, `test_tiny_height_returns_no_content_rows`), which is part of why the two are one slice.

`test/test_screen_layout.rb#test_frame_consumes_layout_body_and_viewport_without_recomputing` MOVED HERE FROM `tui-screen-layout` IN THE 2026-08-02 MERGE REVIEW, and `tui-view-row-projection` was added to `depends_on` for it. At `tui-screen-layout` it was unreachable in both directions at once: it drives `Tui::Frame`, whose slice (this one) depends on `tui-screen-layout`, and it also drives `Tui::Views`, which was upstream of neither. The invariant is that ONE computation feeds both painting and hit testing; these tests can only detect a drift, not prevent it, so the port should keep the single source.

THE READER IS PROVED BY NOTHING, AND IT IS NOT IN THIS SLICE. `Tui::Mouse.decode` is a pure function of one complete report string, so this half is fully provable by translated tests. What no test anywhere covers is the code that gets a complete report out of a byte stream: nothing proves a report split across two reads is reassembled, nothing proves `SEQUENCE` finds a report embedded in a buffer with ordinary keypresses around it, and nothing proves what happens to the bytes of a report the decoder rejected. That reader lives in the app loop, which campaign 12's app-shell group owns; if it has no test there either, this is a hole in the campaign rather than in this slice, and it should be raised as one.

Legacy X10 mouse encoding is DELIBERATELY unsupported and the Ruby says so in a comment pointing at `docs/plans/active/tui-mouse-support.md` — but no test asserts an X10 report is refused. A port that "helpfully" accepts one is green and then mis-decodes every coordinate above 95, because X10 encodes coordinates as single bytes offset by 32. Preserve the refusal deliberately.

`WHEEL_DELTA = 3` is pinned by no test on its own. `test_wheel_over_list_scrolls_list` and `test_every_wheel_target_shares_one_direction` assert the shared DIRECTION, not the magnitude, so a port that scrolls one line per notch passes everything here and feels broken to the user. The value is part of the contract even though every test is about the rule.

The router's decisions are proved against a hand-built `HitMap::Hit`, never against a hit map derived from a real painted frame. That is the correct unit boundary, and it means the two slices can each be right while the pair is wrong — see `tui-hit-map`'s precedence gap for the case that actually bites, a click routed to a widget that is not on top.

THE DECISION TO CLAIM THESE 13 AT ALL, STATED. The shared inventory §5d files `test/test_app_paint_perf.rb` as having "no home in the schema", because `metrics.wall_ms` is "advisory only; never part of conformance equality in either direction" and the RSS and CPU fields are documented as permanently null. That is entirely true of a repaint BUDGET and it is not true of these tests: NOT ONE OF THEM MEASURES TIME. Every assertion is `assert_same`/`refute_same` on object identity, a stubbed call count, or a dirty flag — they are cache-INVALIDATION CORRECTNESS tests wearing a perf file's name. Under this campaign's translated-unit-test method they are exactly as provable as everything else in group B, and leaving them unclaimed would leave the behavior deciding whether the screen goes stale after a filter change, a collapse, a resize or midnight owned by nobody. So: claimed. The gap that remains is the one §5d is actually about — the repaint budget itself is proved by nothing, `perf_budget` is null, and there is no perf gate in the tree to hang one on.

Every test reaches into `Tui::App`'s private state: `instance_variable_get(:@rows)`, `send(:rows)`, `send(:paint_if_needed)`, `@paint_dirty`, `@last_paint_size`, `@row_item_count`. A Go port has no equivalent reach, so the port must expose these seams DELIBERATELY — a row cache with an observable fingerprint, an injectable date provider (the Ruby already has one, `date_provider:`), an injectable winsize reader. If the port hides them instead, this behavior becomes unprovable, and the honest response is to say so in this record rather than let the slice quietly drop to zero tests.

`test_idle_layout_changed_on_terminal_resize` stubs `IO.console.winsize` and `test_idle_layout_changed_on_date_rollover` injects `date_provider`; both BYPASS the determinism pins entirely. `LINES`/`COLUMNS` and `TASKS_PIN_NOW` are the pins that would cover them, and nothing here asserts the app reads either. That is precisely the "a pin that resolves but is not used is invisible" defect class `porting/specs/determinism.md` names and inventory §5a repeats — and the Ruby-only defence (`test/test_porting_determinism_seams.rb`, which patches `Date.today` through `RUBYOPT`) has no Go analogue.

`lib/tui/app.rb` is 3500 lines and its drift closure is 83 files — effectively the whole product, `lib/llm/**` and `lib/term_form/**` included. THIS SLICE PORTS A HANDFUL OF METHODS ON IT, NOT THE FILE. Campaign 12's app-shell group owns `App` proper and names the same file, in the two-owners pattern `campaign-10.md` §6 recorded for `lib/tasks/config.rb`. The practical consequence of the closure size is that this record will read as drifted the moment anything anywhere in the product changes; that is the drift rule working as designed on a file this size, not a reason to narrow `source_paths` below what the behavior actually reads.

`depends_on` names `tui-app-shell`, WHICH GROUP B DID NOT SEED. Campaign 12's app-shell group owns the App lifecycle these methods hang off, and the edge is real — a row cache is meaningless without the loop that asks for rows. The id is group B's best guess at that group's naming, and the merging orchestrator must reconcile it; if the app-shell slice landed under another id, this edge is the one to correct.

THE ROW-CACHE RESET CONTRACT MOVED HERE FROM `tui-app-shell` IN THE 2026-08-02 MERGE REVIEW, with the two tests that were its only oracle there: `test/test_app.rb#test_a_fresh_app_starts_in_the_cleared_cache_state` and `#test_clearing_row_caches_only_assigns_and_needs_no_constructed_state`. Both are Ruby object-model assertions — they reflect over instance variables to prove that clearing the caches assigns and constructs nothing — so a Go port can neither pass nor fail them, and they are kept here rather than dropped only because this slice already owns the PORTABLE oracle for the same contract: `test_clear_row_caches_drops_stale_row_list`, which asserts the observable consequence (a stale row list is not served after a clear) instead of the Ruby mechanism. Characterize against that one. The two moved refs are documentation of the no-allocation intent, not evidence about the port, and a port that satisfies `test_clear_row_caches_drops_stale_row_list` by reconstructing state has met the contract that matters and failed the one that does not travel.

It was upstream of nothing before, so both refs were unreachable where they are claimed. THE `lib/term_form` STANDALONE BOUNDARY IS PART OF THIS SLICE'S CONTRACT AND ITS RUBY TEST IS NOT PORTABLE. test/test_term_form_require_boundary.rb asserts that `require "term_form"` loads nothing from lib/tasks, lib/tui or lib/ansi.rb, and that the bundled examples/term_form_demo.rb names no Tasks or Tui constant. The inventory's OOS list excludes both tests on the correct ground that they are properties of Ruby's $LOADED_FEATURES with no runtime analogue in Go. THE ARCHITECTURAL RULE SURVIVES THE PORT AND IS RECORDED HERE BECAUSE NOTHING ELSE RECORDS IT: the Go package that receives TermForm must not import the tasks or tui packages, and Go enforces that at compile time (an import cycle, or a lint rule over the import graph), not at runtime. The one file outside lib/term_form/ the subsystem is allowed to reach is lib/char_width.rb, the dependency-free width kernel Tui::Ansi also uses; it is in this slice's drift closure transitively and is deliberately kept out of source_paths, because campaign 12 group B's ANSI slice ports it.

THE PENDING-COMMIT STATE MACHINE IS THE WHOLE SLICE AND IT IS PROVED ONLY BY ORDERING, NEVER BY OUTPUT. Eleven of the thirty tests are sequences — a dirty Tab requests a commit and holds focus, a refresh arrives while a commit is pending, the same field refreshes while its buffer is still dirty, an accept carries fresh values or does not, a pending owner is hidden or disabled by reactivity and stays semantically focused until the host resolves it. None of that is a value anything prints; it is a relationship between successive calls. Even if a frame oracle existed it would not see this, which is worth saying plainly: this slice would be unobservable under the differential method for a second, independent reason.

DEFENSIVE COPYING AND DEEP FREEZING ARE ASSERTED AS BEHAVIOR AND MAY NOT SURVIVE TRANSLATION AS MECHANISM. test_values_baselines_and_context_are_defensive_read_only_copies, test_key_map_defensively_copies_mutable_keys and test_custom_struct_values_labels_and_render_data_are_deep_copied_and_frozen assert that a host cannot reach into the engine's state through a returned object. Support#copy / #frozen_copy / #deep_freeze are a Ruby answer to a Ruby problem (everything is a mutable reference). A Go port with value semantics may need none of the machinery and still owes every one of the requirements; the tests must be translated as requirements, not transcribed as `frozen?` assertions.

`porting/manifest-issues reach` is blind to every edge in this slice. Its VERB_OWNERS map covers store mutation verb methods only, so an oracle that reaches downstream through a key handler, a renderer or a form transition is invisible to the tool, and it will keep reporting zero unexplained reaches no matter what campaign 12 claims. campaign-10.md 4g found this and the inventory 5e repeats it for campaigns 6, 9 and 12. Reading the test body is the only defence here.

GRAPHEME AND CELL WIDTH ARE A DATA-TABLE DEPENDENCY THIS SLICE INHERITS AND CANNOT PROVE. THE HINT CONTRACT HAS THREE SHAPES AND ONE OF THEM IS A DELIBERATE SWALLOW. A hint may be a plain string, a zero-or-one-argument callable, or a two-argument callable told how many cells its text may occupy; and a callable that raises must render nothing rather than take the paint loop down, while Form#hint itself still propagates so the failure stays visible to a caller that asks for the value directly. THE THREE INVARIANTS ARE ANTI-JITTER RULES AND EVERY ONE OF THEM IS A NON-CHANGE. Width comes from the FULL content so filtering never resizes the box; the box keeps its full unfiltered height while a filter is active so neither it nor its centred position jumps as matches come and go; replacing live content preserves the user's filter and scroll intent. Four tests exist only to assert the height is retained (test_height_is_retained_while_filtering, test_height_is_retained_even_with_no_matches, test_short_modal_keeps_height_and_shows_matches_while_filtering, test_replacing_live_content_preserves_filter_and_scroll_intent). A port that recomputes geometry from the visible lines is correct on every single frame and wrong in motion — the exact defect class a frame-diff oracle would also have missed.

THE MEMOIZED HAYSTACK IS A PERFORMANCE CONTRACT WITH NO PERFORMANCE GATE. Modal#haystack builds the stripped, downcased view once from the immutable content and memoizes the match set per query, so a keystroke costs one substring scan rather than a fresh ANSI strip of every line on each of view's internal calls. Nothing here asserts it: metrics.wall_ms is advisory only and never part of conformance equality in either direction, and this slice's perf_budget is null. A port that strips per keystroke passes every test in the list and makes the agent-activity modal, whose content is replaced live, visibly laggy. Recorded here because the only campaign 12 file about repaint cost, test/test_app_paint_perf.rb, belongs to group B.

Every one of those is a relationship between two writes separated in time, which the one case, one invocation protocol cannot express even for a CLI, let alone for a TUI.

oracle_gaps: `tasks config --json` prints `tzdb_version`, and its value is `TZInfo::DataSource.get.to_s` — on this host the literal string "Zoneinfo DataSource: /usr/share/zoneinfo", and "Ruby DataSource" on a host carrying the tzinfo-data gem. It is neither a version nor portable: it names a Ruby object and embeds an absolute host path, and no Go port can emit it. determinism.md's exemption does NOT cover this: it exempts the OBSERVATION field `environment.tzdb_version` ("Recorded, never compared for equality"), while this string arrives in `process.stdout`, which `porting/compare` compares byte-for-byte. So every `tasks config --json` case fails on this one key for every implementation, forever — including the cases `config-resolution` already wires, whose `observable_outputs` lists "`tasks config` output" with no gap recorded against it. This is an intentional-difference decision for Marcus (normalize the key, or emit a real tzdb release identifier on both sides); it is recorded here and NOT decided, per PORTING.md.

The runner pins `TZ=UTC` and `TASKS_TIMEZONE=UTC` (`porting/runners/ruby/run`), so nothing in the default pin set ever leaves UTC and every zone-dependent behavior here is unreachable from a fixture alone. It IS reachable: `porting/runners/README.md` says a case's `env` may override any pin, and `invocation.env` records the override, so a case list for this slice must set `TASKS_TIMEZONE` (and `TASKS_PIN_NOW`) per case. That is a case-list obligation, not a harness change — but a corpus built by copying another slice's cases inherits UTC and proves nothing.

`Timezones.detect`'s middle branch reads `/etc/localtime`, follows the symlink, and slices the id out after `/zoneinfo/`. Under the pinned environment `TZ` is always set, so the branch is never taken; and it is host state the copy protocol does not model at all (the eleven copy steps touch the copy root, never `/etc`). `test_timezone_uses_tz_and_detector_reports_utc_fallback` is therefore provable only as a translated unit test with an injected `localtime:` path — the Ruby's own seam — and the real-host branch is proved by nothing on either side. A Go port that reads the host zone by a different mechanism (Go consults `TZ`, then `/etc/localtime`, then the embedded zoneinfo) will disagree here and no conformance run will notice.

The zone REJECTION vocabulary is contract and is easy to lose: `get` refuses a bare identifier with no `/` (except the literal `UTC`) BEFORE asking TZInfo, so "EST" and "PST8PDT" are rejected as `is not an IANA time-zone identifier` even though tzdb knows both. Go's `time.LoadLocation` accepts `EST` and `Local`. A port that delegates straight to `LoadLocation` accepts values this product refuses and writes them into the store, where they become bytes no Ruby reader can validate. `test_unknown_zone_and_abbreviation_are_rejected` is the only oracle for it.

oracle_gaps: The runner pins `TZ=UTC` and `TASKS_TIMEZONE=UTC` (`porting/runners/ruby/run`), so nothing in the default pin set ever leaves UTC and every zone-dependent behavior here is unreachable from a fixture alone. It IS reachable: `porting/runners/README.md` says a case's `env` may override any pin, and `invocation.env` records the override, so a case list for this slice must set `TASKS_TIMEZONE` (and `TASKS_PIN_NOW`) per case. That is a case-list obligation, not a harness change — but a corpus built by copying another slice's cases inherits UTC and proves nothing.

`overdue?` is deliberately asymmetric — `>=` for an all-day value and `>` for a timed one — so a timed deadline is on time AT its exact minute and overdue one second later, while a date-only deadline is overdue from the first instant of the following local date. One comparison operator is the whole behavior, it is invisible in every JSON projection (which reports the derived booleans, not the operator), and the only oracles are `test_timed_deadline_becomes_overdue_immediately_after_its_exact_minute` and `test_all_day_due_boundary_is_next_local_date_not_stored_midnight`. A port that uses `>=` for both passes every fixture in the corpus, because no fixture's `TASKS_PIN_NOW` lands exactly on a stored boundary.

`from_record` is a TWO-STAGE fallback: it tries the full value, and on `ArgumentError`/`KeyError`/`TypeError` retries as a bare date with `validate: false`, and only then returns nil. That is what makes a hand-edited or foreign-writer record read as a date-only task rather than crashing a read. `validate:` defaults to FALSE from a record and TRUE from user input — the same class, two validation regimes, decided by the caller. No claimed test isolates the retry: it is exercised incidentally by `malformed/wrong-types` through `check`. Characterization must capture it directly.

(b) `from_record`'s two-stage lenient retry — the path that accepts a record whose temporal object is partly malformed on a second, tolerant pass — has ZERO tests anywhere in the repository. This slice owns the normalizer that makes those verdicts; it must not re-derive them, and `malformed/recur-non-canonical`'s twenty-seven rows are the shared oracle for both.

`test_rejections_echo_the_input_verbatim` pins that a rejection quotes `raw` (what the user typed) while parsing reads `s` (downcased). A port that echoes the downcased form passes every other test in the file. It is one `echo:` keyword threaded through six methods and it is exactly the parameter a translator drops.

behavior: Projecting a stored recurrence forward: `occurrence_after` for weekly/monthly/yearly with anchor-fixed parity, the month-length clamp vs the skip-when-absent rule, `CYCLE_LIMIT` and the never-fires refusal, and `next_temporal_date`'s civil-time loop with its DST-gap skip and caller veto
oracle_gaps: The runner pins `TZ=UTC` and `TASKS_TIMEZONE=UTC` (`porting/runners/ruby/run`), so nothing in the default pin set ever leaves UTC and every zone-dependent behavior here is unreachable from a fixture alone. It IS reachable: `porting/runners/README.md` says a case's `env` may override any pin, and `invocation.env` records the override, so a case list for this slice must set `TASKS_TIMEZONE` (and `TASKS_PIN_NOW`) per case. That is a case-list obligation, not a harness change — but a corpus built by copying another slice's cases inherits UTC and proves nothing.

The clamp/skip asymmetry is the subtlest rule in the campaign and it is invisible in any single-occurrence output: a NUMERIC day of month clamps to the month's end (`m:31` fires Feb 28) while an ORDINAL weekday a month lacks is SKIPPED entirely (`m:5fri` produces no occurrence in a month without five Fridays, and the search moves to the next cycle). Same file, adjacent lines, opposite policies. A port that clamps both, or skips both, produces a correct-looking next date for most inputs and a wrong series. `test_numeric_day_a_month_lacks_clamps_to_the_month_end` and `test_ordinal_weekday_a_month_lacks_skips_to_a_month_that_has_one` are the pair; neither is observable without a series.

PARITY is anchored on the STORED stamp, not on the clock, for every `Nw`/`Nm`/`Ny` form — `weekly_after` derives the anchor's ISO Monday and counts whole blocks from it. So the same schedule fires on different dates from different anchors, and a schedule can be unsatisfiable for one anchor and fine for another (`2y:02:5fri` needs a February with five Fridays, which only some leap years give, so an odd-parity anchor never fires). That is why `no_occurrence` raises with the anchor named. A port that anchors parity on today passes every single-occurrence assertion and drifts on the second.

`next_temporal_date` is bounded by a literal 1000 iterations and RESCUES `Timezones::Error`/`ArgumentError` inside the loop, which is how a candidate landing in a DST gap advances to the following occurrence instead of raising. Neither the bound nor the swallowed exception is observable: a correct implementation and one that raises on the first gap differ only on a store whose stamp lands in a gap, and no fixture's does. `test_dst_gap_candidate_skips_to_the_next_occurrence` and `test_next_temporal_date_keeps_nw_parity_when_a_candidate_hits_a_dst_gap` need a case-level `TASKS_TIMEZONE` override to be anything but unit tests.

The `yield`-based veto (`test_validation_block_can_veto_a_calendar_candidate`) is a Ruby block passed by `Store#advance_recurrence_records` so a paired field landing in a gap can reject a candidate the schedule accepts. It is an in-process callback with no wire representation at all; the port's shape for it (a func parameter) is an interface decision this slice must make and record, because `store-recurrence-advance` is its only caller and depends on it.
fixtures_todo: `valid/recur-calendar-grammar` carries every canonical FORM but each record's stamp is chosen to be valid, not to be interesting: nothing in the corpus has an anchor from which its own schedule can never fire, and nothing has a stamp years stale. Needed, as one small `valid/recur-anchors` fixture: (a) a record with `recur: 2y:02:5fri` on an odd-parity anchor (the never-fires case, whose refusal names the anchor), (b) the same schedule on a leap-parity anchor (the control), (c) a `w:mon` record whose stamp is ~2000 days behind the pinned now (the catch-up walk), and (d) a `m:5fri` record anchored in a month with no fifth Friday (the skip). All four are reachable through `tasks recur <ref>` (preview) with no writes, so they cost one fixture and no protocol change. Four later slices need the same store; build it once.

behavior: The lead-time span grammar: the canonical `<count><unit>` form and its zero exclusion, friendly-phrase and abbreviation parsing with filler-word removal, `off` clearing, the calendar/clock unit split (`m` is months, never minutes), humanization, the derived gate date and its month clamp, the clock duration and its raw instant arithmetic, and the deadline-before-scheduled anchor precedence
oracle_gaps: `gate_instant` is documented as RAW on purpose — it subtracts seconds from the anchor's instant and deliberately does NOT rebuild a `TemporalValue`, because rebuilding would re-resolve an ambiguous local time and could move the gate by an hour across a DST fall-back. That is a negative requirement: the correct implementation is defined by what it does not do, and both implementations produce the same answer on every non-DST date. Only `test_a_clock_lead_crossing_dst_keeps_its_duration_not_its_wall_time` separates them, and it needs a case-level `TASKS_TIMEZONE` override to be anything but a unit test.

The absence of a minute unit is contract, not an omission. `CLOCK_WORDS` carries `h`/`hr`/`hrs`/`hour`/`hours` and deliberately omits `m`/`min`, because `m` means months in both this grammar and the recurrence grammar and overloading it would silently change what an existing STORED value means. A port that adds minutes for convenience reinterprets every `5m` lead already on disk. `test_hour_leads_parse_and_m_still_means_months` is the only oracle.

`parse_phrase` has a fall-through a reader will not expect: a single token that is not in `WORDS` but IS in `CLOCK_WORDS` returns `[1, "h"]`, so a bare "hour" means one hour while a bare "day" goes through `WORDS`. Two lookup tables, one of which supplies its own implicit count. Covered incidentally by the claimed parse tests; characterization must isolate it.

'THE CLOCK DURATION AND ITS RAW INSTANT ARITHMETIC' — `Lead.duration` and `Lead.gate_instant` — IS DECLARED HERE AND EXERCISED SOLELY BY `lead-availability-gate`, WHICH DEPENDS ON THIS SLICE. None of the seven refs claimed here reaches either method: they cover the span grammar, the `off` words, the zero/junk refusals, `m`-means-months, humanization, the month/year clamp and the anchor precedence, and all of them stop at the parsed span. The instant arithmetic is only observable once a gate is evaluated, which is the downstream slice's subject. No legal edge fixes a downstream-only oracle and the clause is kept because the arithmetic is real. What a port can get wrong while staying green here: computing a clock lead by subtracting whole days from the anchor's DATE instead of the stated duration from the anchor's INSTANT — every test claimed here passes, and the gate opens on the wrong side of local midnight in exactly the cases `lead-availability-gate` covers.

The release boundary is INCLUSIVE (`released?` is `context.now >= release_instant`) while `overdue?` for a timed value is strictly `>`. The gap that remains is real and belongs here: `TemporalValue#due_boundary` — ordering by the exact release/due INSTANT rather than by date — has NO oracle on the domain side. A port of this slice can compute `due_boundary` at date granularity and stay green through the whole Ruby suite, because the only test that would notice sorts through the TUI renderer instead. behavior: The lead window as a read: `TaskQueries#lead_gate` — the calendar gate at local midnight of the derived date, the clock gate at an exact instant, the anchor's own zone deciding a fixed anchor's midnight, ancestor leads gating a subtree, the later-gate-wins rule against other blockers, and an own hold outranking a lead
oracle_gaps: The runner pins `TZ=UTC` and `TASKS_TIMEZONE=UTC` (`porting/runners/ruby/run`), so nothing in the default pin set ever leaves UTC and every zone-dependent behavior here is unreachable from a fixture alone. It IS reachable: `porting/runners/README.md` says a case's `env` may override any pin, and `invocation.env` records the override, so a case list for this slice must set `TASKS_TIMEZONE` (and `TASKS_PIN_NOW`) per case. That is a case-list obligation, not a harness change — but a corpus built by copying another slice's cases inherits UTC and proves nothing.

A CALENDAR lead holds its wall DATE across a DST change while a CLOCK lead holds its DURATION and therefore moves its wall time. That contrast is the point of the pair and it is one test each (`test_a_calendar_lead_holds_its_wall_date_across_a_dst_change`, `test_a_clock_lead_crossing_dst_keeps_its_duration_not_its_wall_time`). Both are unreachable under the UTC pin; both need a case with `TASKS_TIMEZONE: "America/Denver"` and a `TASKS_PIN_NOW` on either side of 2026-03-08 and 2026-11-01. A port that implements one rule for both units passes every UTC case in the corpus.

A lead's gate for a FIXED anchor opens at midnight in the ANCHOR's zone, not the reader's (`test_a_timezone_carrying_anchor_opens_at_midnight_in_the_anchors_zone`), while a floating or all-day anchor opens at midnight in the reader's. So the same record is available at different instants for two readers in different zones, by design, and the corpus — pinned to one zone — cannot show the difference at all. This is the sharpest instance of the campaign's zone-pin limitation and the reason the fixtures_todo below asks for a zoned anchor.

`Lead.display` returns the span ALONE when it is a clock span and no context is supplied, rather than guessing a zone. That is a rendering decision made inside the model, so it is this slice's rather than campaign 8's, and it is proved only by `test_a_clock_lead_carries_its_own_window_onto_the_task_view`.

`test_lead_matrix.rb#test_project_header_counts_agree_with_the_read_model` is SPLIT and is now claimed by two slices, deliberately (the 2026-08-02 merge review). Its `work.open_count == 3` / `work.held_count == 0` asserts — a timed gate is not an indefinite hold — are this slice's and are the reason it is claimed here. Its other half compares `V.rows(:projects, …)` header TEXT against the roll-up, which is `Tui::Views` and belongs to `tui-view-row-projection`, where it is also claimed. The consequence for characterization here: only the counts are this slice's oracle, so a capture must assert the `ProjectView` roll-up directly rather than through the rendered header, or a renderer change will read as a lead-gate defect.

oracle_gaps: This is the campaign's genuine determinism gap and it must be stated exactly, not inflated. The pins themselves are fine: `TASKS_PIN_NOW` covers every clock read in campaign 5 (they are all wall-clock and all persisted), and determinism.md's own note that `invocation.pins[].applied` records RESOLUTION rather than USE is answered on the Ruby side by `test/test_porting_determinism_seams.rb`, which intercepts `Date.today`/`Time.now`/`Socket.gethostname`/`SecureRandom` at the source via `RUBYOPT=-r` and fails on any read the pins should have removed. That defence is Ruby-only: it is a monkeypatch of the language's own clock API, it has no analogue in a compiled binary, and the observation schema records nothing that would substitute. So on the Go side the claim 'every temporal call site received the injected today' is UNPROVABLE by conformance alone. What remains provable is narrower and still worth having: that a single invocation's outputs are mutually consistent — the parsed date, the written stamp, the history label and the JSON all agree — which is exactly what the four claimed `*_uses_one_today_*` tests assert, and which a wall-clock leak breaks whenever an invocation straddles midnight. A port needs a Go-side equivalent of the seams test (a build-tagged clock interface with a fake that records every read); that is new harness work, not translation.

`Tasks::Application` has some thirty methods with a `today: Date.today` DEFAULT PARAMETER, which determinism.md names as the shipped defect class: one adapter call site that forgets to pass `today:` produces wall-clock output with `applied: true` recorded beside it. A Go port has no default parameters, so the direct translation is a nil-check with the same failure mode. Making `today` a required field of an explicit context — which would make the defect impossible — is refactoring-while-translating and is forbidden here without a decision; it is recorded as a candidate for Marcus rather than taken.

behavior: The store's advisory file lock and its complement, external-change detection: an flock on the `.<basename>.lock` sidecar beside the symlink-resolved live file, created by reads as well as writes, reentrant per (Thread, Fiber) execution context, refusing cross-Fiber contention rather than blocking, plus `Store#changed?` and the read model's `stale?` for the out-of-band edits the lock deliberately does not constrain
oracle_gaps: NO OBSERVATION FIELD RECORDS A LOCK BEING ACQUIRED — only that a sidecar appeared. porting/specs/determinism.md keeps `.tasks.jsonl.lock` in `files.deltas` on purpose (a READ against a pristine copy is not delta-free: it emits {"path": ".tasks.jsonl.lock", "kind": "created"}), so the harness sees that a file appeared and cannot see that mutual exclusion held, that flock(LOCK_EX) was called rather than the file merely opened, that the descriptor stayed open across the read-modify-write, or that the lock was released. A port that opens the sidecar RDWR|CREAT, never locks, and writes emits a BYTE-IDENTICAL observation to a correct one on every single-process case in the corpus. `adversarial/stale-lock-sidecar` narrows this from one side only: it proves the port did not implement a lock-file-EXISTS protocol (such a port deadlocks on a perfectly available store), never that a real lock was taken.

ONE CASE IS ONE INVOCATION, so four of this slice's six tests have no differential path at all. porting/runners/README.md's case list has one argv, one process, one before/after pair, and no vocabulary for a second process, a second invocation against the same copy, an interleaving, or an ordering. test_concurrent_writers_do_not_lose_updates spawns eight `tasks capture` processes at once; test_cli_claim_race_leaves_exactly_one_holder races two claims; test_with_lock_rejects_cross_fiber_contention_and_cleans_up and test_shared_store_reads_stay_coherent_across_threads live inside one process, in Fibers and Threads the protocol cannot address. All four are provable by translated unit tests only — the honest-but-not-differential position agent-request-queue occupies in campaign 10. This is also why PORTING.md's high tier asks for 'real competing processes' SEPARATELY from differential conformance: for this slice that separate obligation is the only proof there is.

test_with_lock_rejects_cross_fiber_contention_and_cleans_up has NO conformance expression whatsoever, not merely a weak one. It asserts that a second Fiber on the owning thread raises CrossFiberLockError instead of blocking — because a Fiber that waits on its own thread's flock prevents the owner from resuming to release it. There is no case-list key for a second Fiber and no observation field that would record the refusal if there were. The Go port has no Fiber, so the rule must be re-expressed for goroutines during characterization rather than translated; the invariant to preserve is 'contention that cannot make progress is refused explicitly, never waited on'.

Store#changed? is stat-based and its token must NOT be compared. test_changed_detects_external_writes calls File.utime(future, future, org) with its own comment saying 'avoid same-mtime flakiness'; filesystem timestamp granularity is not in porting/specs/determinism.md's pin table and cannot be. A port using a different staleness token (a revision compare, an inode+size pair) is not wrong and will not match a byte-level expectation of the token. Compare the DECISION (stale? true/false) and treat the token as internal.

Atomic replacement is NOT this slice's and NOT this campaign's, despite the playbook's campaign 6 line. store-canonical-write (campaign 4) owns lib/tasks/atomic.rb and the eight test_atomic_write_* cases at the top of test/test_journal.rb, which is why that file is 32 unclaimed of 40. This slice touches the same territory at exactly one point and defers to that record for the other half: Store#lock_path resolves the sidecar name through Journal.canonical while Atomic.resolve resolves the temp sibling, so against `valid/symlinked-store` BOTH must land on the target name (.tasks.real.jsonl.lock). store-canonical-write's gaps already state the write half and the literal 0o644 lock-mode divergence on a 0600 store; this slice proves the lock half and adds nothing to atomic.rb.

Cross-process concurrency through HTTP is campaign 9's, not this slice's, and the boundary is which side of Store#with_lock the test observes from (inventory §3e). test/api/test_black_box.rb spawns a real bin/tasks-api with Process.spawn and races an API thread against a CLI thread; what it proves is that the SERVER observes a CLI write, a property of the HTTP adapter's read model and its ETag. It is deliberately not claimed here. The symmetric trap is recorded so campaign 9 does not claim test_concurrent_writers_do_not_lose_updates: it is the same invariant seen through two adapters and the port needs both proofs.

A documented limit in the Ruby that the port must decide about rather than inherit silently: the reentrancy guard is per Store INSTANCE, so two Stores on the same file in one thread would deadlock in flock with no diagnostic (flock excludes across fds within one process). The Ruby says no such nesting exists today and that a fiber-scheduler server would need a process-wide registry keyed on lock_path. No test covers it, nothing in the corpus can reach it, and a Go port with a package-level registry would be BETTER and DIFFERENT — an intentional-difference record for Marcus, not something to land while translating.

THE SYMLINK-RESOLVED LOCK PATH IS ASSERTED BY NO TEST IN THE REPOSITORY, AND IT IS THE HIGHEST-CONSEQUENCE UNPROVED CLAUSE FOUND IN THIS CAMPAIGN. The behavior sentence and `observable_outputs` both name the sidecar beside the SYMLINK-RESOLVED live file (`.tasks.real.jsonl.lock` for a store reached through `tasks.jsonl` -> `tasks.real.jsonl`). The only test that touches the path is `test/test_store.rb:242`, which reads `store.send(:lock_path)` and compares it to itself — a tautology that any value satisfies. Verified 2026-08-02. What a port can get wrong while staying green through the ENTIRE Ruby suite: locking beside the symlink rather than beside its target. Two processes reaching one store through two path spellings then take two different locks, believe they hold exclusion, and interleave writes — the exact failure the lock exists to prevent, produced by a port that passes every test. Note the journal already resolves `realpath` for its directory key and `journal-index-and-blobs` records that ITS key is unpinned too: the two gaps are the same missing property, and a port that resolves one and not the other is internally inconsistent as well as wrong.

`test/test_cli_mutations.rb#test_cli_claim_race_leaves_exactly_one_holder` WAS DROPPED FROM THIS SLICE BY THE 2026-08-02 MERGE REVIEW: despite the name, nothing in it races. Its three `run_cli_at` calls are strictly sequential, and every assertion is delegation compare-and-set text — the conflict message, the `{error, action, holder, at}` JSON, the final assignee. Remove the lock from the store entirely and the test still passes, which is the definition of a misattributed oracle. The genuinely concurrent case, `test/test_delegation.rb#test_concurrent_claims_across_stores_leave_exactly_one_holder`, is already owned by `delegation-claim-release` and is upstream of nothing this slice needs. What the drop costs: this slice's 'store bytes after N concurrent writers' observable now rests on `test_journal.rb#test_concurrent_writers_do_not_lose_updates` alone.
fixtures_todo: The corpus can show the sidecar appearing; it cannot show exclusion, and nothing new would change that under the current protocol (see the one-case-one-invocation gap), so no new fixture is requested. What IS owed at the case level and does not exist: a read-only case against `valid/small-gtd` whose expected deltas are exactly [.tasks.jsonl.lock created], pinning the 'a read creates the lock' rule determinism.md deliberately refused to normalize away; and one case each against `valid/symlinked-store` and `valid/restricted-mode-store` asserting the sidecar's resolved NAME and its literal 0644 mode. Those three are the whole observable surface of this slice. ALSO (2026-08-02): `valid/symlinked-store` already ships the shape needed to close the symlink-resolved-lock gap above, and nothing is wired to it here. One case — any mutation against the store reached through its SYMLINK spelling — makes the sidecar's resolved name an ordinary `files.deltas` entry: Ruby creates `.tasks.real.jsonl.lock` beside the target and a port that locks beside the link creates `.tasks.jsonl.lock` instead, which the comparator sees as a created-path mismatch. This is a one-case fixture wiring, not new corpus work, and it converts the campaign's most dangerous unfalsifiable clause into a diff.

the sidecar's resolved name against a symlinked store (`.tasks.real.jsonl.lock`)
