notes: Ports Store#with_lock, Store#lock_path, Store#changed? and Application::ReadModel#stale? out of lib/tasks/store.rb and lib/tasks/application.rb — nine and two other slices respectively own the rest of those files, and this record ports only those methods. lib/tasks/journal.rb is named because lock_path resolves through Journal.canonical, not because this slice ports the journal. First of eleven campaign 6 slices and deliberately separate from the checked-write slice below it: its failure modes are concurrency reviews (reentrancy key, explicit refusal instead of a block, per-instance scope) rather than persistence reviews, and PORTING.md wants those in different sittings. Windows has no flock; LockFileEx is the analogue and its semantics around inherited handles differ — the platform risk to surface here rather than discover at cutover.

behavior: Computing the three-component task revision `v1.<own>.<location>.<lifecycle>`: which fields feed each SHA-256 digest, date and hash normalization before digesting, the bulk sibling index that must agree with the inline scan, and the deliberate absence of a line-number or mtime fallback for id-less records
oracle_gaps: THE TASK REVISION IS IN NO OBSERVATION FIELD AS A VALUE THIS SLICE PRODUCES. porting/specs/observations.schema.json carries `revisions.store`, `revisions.resources` and `revisions.touched_ids` — the store-wide token from the after-probe, and the ids the implementation's own --json payload reported. `adversarial/stale-revision` ships revisions.json with per-task tokens, which is what makes that fixture a fixture; but a task revision reaches an observation only when a command prints one. A port that computed the three components over the WRONG field sets but did so consistently would satisfy every staleness comparison in this campaign's later slices and differ only in the literal digest — visible against the fixture's recorded tokens and nowhere else. Characterize against revisions.json, not through a verb.

Positional gap, in the shape campaign-10.md §4g named and `reach` cannot see: test_location_fingerprint_conflicts_on_structural_change_but_not_field_change reaches Store#patch_task!, owned by changeset-apply-basic, which is NOT upstream of this slice and deliberately is not made one. The revision is computed when the read snapshot is built (Store#task_revisions), three edges upstream of any patch; the patch is only how this test OBSERVES that a structural change moved the location component while a field change did not. The ref is kept because it is the clearest oracle in the suite for the location fingerprint's content, and characterization must drive location_fingerprint directly rather than through a patch verb this slice does not own.

The three components' field sets ARE the slice and none of them is enumerated by any test. `own` covers REVISION_OWN_FIELDS plus scheduled_time, deadline_time and the delegation marker (ADR-0007, so an HTTP If-Match claim uses the same component every field edit does); `location` covers the parent, the sibling id list and the subtree's (type, id, parent) structure; `lifecycle` covers the subtree's tasks' id/parent/state/closed/scheduled/scheduled_time/deadline/deadline_time/recur and whether the DEFER tag is present. A port that omitted scheduled_time from `own`, or the DEFER flag from `lifecycle`, passes all three tests here and then silently permits a stale zone edit or a stale defer toggle to overwrite a fresh one. Characterization must pin the field sets themselves against `adversarial/stale-revision`.

Time metadata is hashed as the STORED objects only, never as derived instants — the Ruby says why: 'so a tzdata update cannot invalidate revisions'. That is the one place this slice touches campaign 5's territory and it must not be ported as 'resolve then hash'. porting/specs/determinism.md records that environment.tzdb_version is captured and never compared, so a port that hashed resolved instants would produce revisions that differ between two correct implementations and the harness would report it as a defect it is not.

`sibling_ids_by_parent` is a performance index and a correctness hazard: the Ruby's own comment says it 'must yield the exact id list the inline scan produces, or the same task would carry different revisions depending on which path built it'. Two code paths, one required answer, and no test drives both against the same store. A port that keeps only one path removes the hazard and is a legitimate simplification to record as an intentional difference rather than to make by accident.

THE `lifecycle` COMPONENT AND THE `own` COMPOSITION HAVE NO ORACLE AT ANY POSITION IN THE GRAPH. Verified by mutation, 2026-08-02: a constant `lifecycle` digest — the same 64 hex characters for every task — passes all three tests claimed here; a port that emits a revision token for an id-less record instead of `nil` passes all three; and this record's own earlier admission that dropping `scheduled_time` from the `own` digest 'passes all three tests here' is TRUE. The two candidate real oracles do not rescue it: one is bucketed PRIOR and is claimed by no slice, the other belongs to a slice DOWNSTREAM of this one. So the behavior sentence's 'which fields feed each SHA-256 digest' is, for two of the three components, an unfalsifiable claim. What a port can get wrong while staying green: any field may be added to or removed from `own` or `lifecycle` without detection, which produces a token that looks well-formed, compares equal across an edit a user made, and silently defeats every If-Match precondition and stale-revision refusal built on top of it. This is the highest-consequence unproved clause in campaign 6 after `store-file-lock`'s.
fixtures_todo: `adversarial/stale-revision` is the only fixture that pins revision tokens and it pins two changed tasks and one unchanged one, which proves the token moves and not WHICH component moved. Owed: an extension of that fixture's revisions.json (or a sibling fixture) recording, for one task, the token before and after four separate edits — a title change (own only), a sibling reorder (location only), a descendant state change (lifecycle only), and a scheduled_time-only edit (own, and the case a port is most likely to drop). Four before/after pairs against one store make the field sets falsifiable; today nothing does. ALSO (2026-08-02): an `adversarial/revision-component-matrix` corpus built to close the gap above — one base store plus a family of single-field variants, exactly one field changed per variant, covering every field claimed to feed `own` (including `scheduled_time` and the zone objects) and every field claimed to feed `lifecycle`, plus one record with no `id` at all. Driven as `tasks show --json` (or any read that emits the token), the case set makes each component's field membership a diff: a port whose `own` omits a field emits an UNCHANGED token for the variant that changes it, which the comparator sees immediately. This is the only shape that turns 'which fields feed each digest' from prose into evidence, and it costs no harness capability.
observable_outputs: the literal `v1.<64hex>.<64hex>.<64hex>` token per task
which of the three components changes across a given edit
nil rather than a token for an id-less record
notes: Ports Store#task_revision / #task_revisions / #location_fingerprint / #lifecycle_fingerprint / #revision_value / #semantic_digest out of lib/tasks/store.rb only; nine other slices name that file and none ports these methods. Tiered medium, deliberately and against this campaign's grain: it computes a digest from an in-memory record list and writes nothing, which is campaign 3's shape rather than campaign 4's. The comparison rules that USE the token are the two slices after it and both are high. The expected defect is a port that digests Go-idiomatic serializations rather than the normalized structures the Ruby builds — revision_value sorts hash keys by name and renders Dates as ISO8601 precisely so the digest cannot depend on the language's map ordering or date rendering.

behavior: The checked-write envelope every mutation runs inside (`Store#with_history`): snapshot both files, run the mutation, and record history only when it actually wrote AND changed bytes; on a post-write Check failure or a writer failure, record the reason, restore both files, and report failure instead — including the diagnostic's deliberate refusal to name the file, the validation reason, or the underlying exception
oracle_gaps: `files.rolled_back` IS NULL UNLESS THE CALLER ASKED FOR --json, and this slice's entire subject is the distinction that field exists to record. porting/runners/README.md: the value is read from the implementation's own --json error envelope, 'never inferred from stderr wording, and never from the deltas: a write-then-revert and a never-wrote leave identical bytes, which is why the field exists' — and its known-gaps list adds that null means 'not reported' and NEVER 'did not roll back'. So on every case that does not pass --json, the observation is silent about which of this slice's two outcomes occurred, and the two outcomes are byte-identical by construction. Every case characterizing this slice must pass --json or it proves nothing about rollback.

TWO OF THE THREE NEWEST TESTS ASSERT ABSENCES THE SCHEMA CANNOT EXPRESS. test_a_failed_write_never_blames_validation asserts the diagnostic does NOT contain 'failed validation after the edit' and does NOT contain 'tasks check'; test_a_failed_write_diagnostic_carries_no_path_and_no_exception_text asserts stderr, stdout and the JSON `message` all omit the run's own absolute directory, 'rb_sysopen' and 'Permission denied'. A byte comparison of stderr catches a port emitting the wrong string only when the baseline was captured at the same absolute path — and the path is precisely what must not be there. The absence assertions survive translation as unit tests; they do not survive as a diff. This is the failure mode a port WILL have: Go's os.PathError stringifies to `open /abs/path/tasks.jsonl: permission denied` by default, leaking both the path and the errno text in one line.

THE ONLY ROUTE TO A PERFORMED-THEN-REVERTED WRITE NEEDS A CASE KEY NO CASE USES. porting/runners/README.md § 'A failing write' is explicit: a store that is already invalid is refused by the PREFLIGHT, which validates the same file set the post-write check does, so post-write validation can never fire from fixture content alone. The reachable route is an unwritable copy root whose lock sidecar already exists, via `copy_root_mode` — a key defined in the protocol and used by zero cases today. Until such a case exists every rollback property here is proved by translated unit tests only. The README also states the ceiling plainly: copy_root_mode 'buys exactly one crash point — the write — from outside the process', against the playbook's step 7 which wants crash points around lock, write, flush, validation, rename AND journal append. Six wanted, one available.

THE ATOMICITY THIS SLICE'S RECOVERY RESTS ON IS ITSELF UNOBSERVABLE. Store#rollback_history_files retries 'because atomic replacement means a failed attempt leaves either the complete old or complete new file' — the Ruby's own comment. But files.deltas carries only {path, kind, before_sha256, after_sha256} and files.after carries mode and content: there is NO field for durability, for the temp sibling (determinism.md: temp filenames 'are gone before an observation is taken'), for the directory fsync, or for the rename. A port that writes in place, correctly, emits an observation identical in every byte to one that writes a temp sibling, fsyncs it, fsyncs the parent, and renames. That port's rollbacks then produce torn state and no case in the corpus can tell. Atomic replacement is store-canonical-write's (campaign 4, inventory §3f) and is not re-sliced here; this gap records that this slice INHERITS its unprovenness.

The rollback wordings are adjacent to store-repair's and must not be collapsed. store-repair's gap already records the pair it owns — a preflight refusal says 'task file is already invalid — run `tasks check` (nothing was written)' and a rolled-back write says 'file failed validation after the edit'. This slice owns a THIRD: a write that FAILED, rather than validated badly, must say 'nothing was changed' and must NOT say either of the other two. td-d6ed92 records that collapsing these looks like a harmless simplification. Three wordings, three causes, and two tests here assert the ABSENCE of the other two because that is the failure mode a port will have.

The no-op rule is subtler than 'skip the write' and is asserted from two directions. with_history records history only when the result is truthy AND non-zero AND the after-snapshot differs from the before-snapshot; a typed refusal that inspected a preexisting invalid file to report an actionable conflict wrote nothing, so its result is PRESERVED rather than turned into a validation failure. test_noop_mutation_records_no_history (an idempotent tag re-add) and test_failed_mutation_records_no_history are the two halves. A port that runs post_write_failure unconditionally converts every honest refusal on an already-invalid store into a rollback report.

TWO CORRECTIONS FROM THE 2026-08-02 MERGE REVIEW. (a) `test/test_task_changeset.rb#test_one_field_task_patch_uses_the_shared_changeset_history_path` was dropped and moved to `changeset-apply-basic`: it discriminates routing and labelling, and changing nothing inside `with_history`, `snapshot` or `restore` leaves it passing. (b) Four of this slice's refs — `test_changeset_result_carries_immutable_post_write_read_snapshot`, `test_cli_reports_a_post_write_rollback_from_the_application_store`, `test_a_failed_write_is_reported_as_rolled_back_with_the_file_unchanged` and `test_a_failed_write_diagnostic_carries_no_path_and_no_exception_text` — drive `capture --json` and assert the `rolled_back` field of an envelope owned by `cli-mutation-json-envelopes`, which is NOT upstream. The edge was considered and rejected: this slice's checked write does not need the CLI's JSON envelopes to function, `cli-mutation-json-envelopes` transitively depends on eight campaign-3/4 mutation slices, and `manifest.md` requires an edge to be true rather than convenient. So the envelope SHAPE is not proved here; characterization must assert the rollback at the store return value (`MutationResult`'s rollback stage and its restored bytes) and treat the `--json` field as an incidental rendering of it.

UNDO IS USED HERE AS AN ASSERTION MECHANISM, NOT AS A DEPENDENCY, AND THAT IS WHY NO EDGE TO `undo-redo-apply` IS DECLARED. `porting/manifest-issues reach` gained `undo!` / `redo!` / `repair!` in its `VERB_OWNERS` table on 2026-08-02, which surfaced these refs for the first time; the 2026-08-02 merge review read each one and classified it as a reach to EXPLAIN rather than an edge to add. `undo-redo-apply` depends on this slice (directly or transitively), so the edge would be a cycle in most of these cases and a false claim in the rest: this slice's behavior does not require undo to work, the tests merely use undo to observe whether a history entry was recorded. The instruction `manifest.md`'s `reach` section prescribes applies verbatim — characterization must drive the behavior at its own level. The four remaining reaching refs — `test_successful_patch_is_one_undoable_checked_write`, `test_post_write_check_failure_rolls_back_and_records_no_history`, `test_writer_failure_rolls_back_and_records_no_history` and `test_post_write_check_failure_rolls_back_placement_and_records_no_history` — are the sharpest case of the pattern, because 'records no history' is literally an assertion about the journal made through the undo verb. This slice ports `with_history`, the thing that decides whether an entry is recorded, so the correct capture is at that seam: the journal index before and after, which the observation schema records directly and which needs no undo at all. Only `test_successful_patch_is_one_undoable_checked_write` asserts a restore, and the byte-exactness it checks is a property of what the checked write stored.

Owed: at least two cases against `valid/small-gtd` with `copy_root_mode: "0555"` and the lock sidecar pre-created — one plain (`tasks capture ...`) pinning stderr's 'nothing was changed' and the absence of the validation wording, one with --json pinning `files.rolled_back` and the {error, action, message} envelope whose `message` must contain neither the copy root nor an errno string. `copy_root_mode` exists in the protocol and no case uses it. notes: Ports Store#with_history, #post_write_failure, #snapshot, #restore, #restore_file and the rollback record/report seam out of lib/tasks/store.rb, plus the CLI's rendering of a rollback in bin/tasks and the Application store's propagation of it — nine other slices name store.rb, five name bin/tasks, and none ports these. Everything in campaign 6 above it (the journal, undo/redo, coalescing) hangs off with_history, which is why it sits third rather than later. The expected defect is ordering: a port that records history BEFORE post-write validation leaves an undo step pointing at bytes that were rolled back, and every green-path test still passes. The four rollback-STAGE tests in test/test_create_task.rb are claimed here rather than by create-basic: they were added by b3d297c (td-fea097), which post-dates the campaigns-5-6-9-12 inventory, and what they pin is which stage failed — the write-vs-validation distinction this slice exists to prove — not task creation.

behavior: Expected-revision checking for a task changeset: which of the three revision components each change set requires (`own` always, `location` when moving by legacy order, `lifecycle` when touching state), the typed :stale result and its interaction with confirmations, and the rule that a strict-revision changeset never takes the targeted-repair branch
oracle_gaps: THE ASYMMETRY IS THE SLICE AND A CONSERVATIVE PORT LOOKS CORRECT. Store#changeset_revision_error requires `own` always, adds `location` only when the changeset moves by legacy order (NOT when it carries a TaskPlacement), and adds `lifecycle` only when it touches :state. A port that compares all three components on every edit refuses edits Ruby accepts — a title change on a task whose sibling was reordered, a body change under a descendant whose state moved — and every test in changeset-apply-basic still passes, because those tests supply nil expected revisions. The two tests that pin the asymmetry (test_title_only_changeset_ignores_a_sibling_change_but_state_guards_lifecycle, test_state_adopts_an_unrelated_body_change) are the only oracle for it in the suite.

A STALE REFUSAL AND A SUCCESSFUL NO-OP LEAVE IDENTICAL STORE BYTES, and the observation distinguishes them only through exit status and stdout. There is no observation field for a typed mutation status; `files.rolled_back` is null unless --json was asked for (porting/runners/README.md known gaps: null means 'not reported', never 'did not roll back'), and `files.mutated` is false in both cases. Every conformance case for this slice must therefore drive a CLI verb under --json and compare the envelope, or it compares an empty delta list against an empty delta list.

NO FIXTURE FEEDS AN EXPECTED REVISION INTO A COMMAND. `adversarial/stale-revision` ships revisions.json with genuinely stale tokens beside a post-edit store, which is the input this slice needs — but a case's only inputs are argv, env and stdin, so a case must PASTE a literal token from that file into argv. That is workable and is what the fixtures_todo asks for; it is recorded as a gap because it makes every case here brittle against any change to the fixture's store bytes, and because a port whose revision digest differs from Ruby's (see store-revision-token) cannot use the corpus's tokens at all and will report every such case as stale. Characterize the port's own token first.

test_nil_location_resolves_current_enclosing_section_under_mutation_lock is claimed here rather than with placement because what it asserts is a staleness rule stated as a resolution rule: a nil location resolves the enclosing section from the LIVE records read under the mutation lock, not from the caller's snapshot. It is the one test in the campaign that ties store-file-lock and the revision comparison together, and a port that resolves from the snapshot passes it whenever nothing changed in between — which is every single-process case in the corpus.

test_strict_revision_changeset_never_repairs_an_invalid_file is the interaction with campaign 4's targeted repair and it is stated as a NEGATIVE. Store#apply_task_changeset! grants the repair branch only when the changeset is NOT strict-revision and repair_scope? attributes every preflight error to the target record; changeset-apply-basic owns the positive case (test_patch_repairs_only_when_every_error_is_on_the_targeted_record) and this slice owns the exclusion. store-repair (campaign 4) is the neighbouring class-level answer and is deliberately NOT a dependency here: `tasks repair` and this branch are different mechanisms that must not converge — a port that let a strict-revision edit repair would silently rewrite records the caller never saw.

test/test_lead_matrix.rb is not free: inventory §3j splits it four C5 / three C12 / one C6. Only test_a_lead_write_conflicts_like_any_other_field is claimed here, because it sits under the file's own '-- concurrency --' heading and asserts that a lead write is an ordinary own-component conflict with no special case. The other seven belong to campaigns 5 and 12 and must not be swept in because the file's name looks temporal.

behavior: The on-disk undo journal's shape and identity: the XDG_STATE_HOME directory keyed by sha256(realpath(org))[0,16], the `org` guard recorded inside index.json, content-addressed deduplicated blobs, the states/cursor timeline, redo-tail truncation, the undo-limit cap and the blob garbage collection that follows it — and the rule that two spellings of one file share one history while two files never do
oracle_gaps: THE JOURNAL INDEX'S `org` KEY FORCES SAME-ABSOLUTE-PATH RUNS, AND THIS SLICE MUST NOT DISCOVER IT LATE. index.json records the store's canonical absolute path, and unlike the directory key that value sits INSIDE bytes the harness digests. porting/specs/determinism.md refuses to normalize it — 'rewriting bytes before digesting them is exactly the move that makes a byte comparison stop meaning anything' — and solves it by running 'both sides against copies at the same absolute path (sequentially, or via a per-side mount)'. Two consequences: (1) a --cross-path run is compared WITH THE JOURNAL INDEX EXCLUDED, which excludes precisely the bytes this slice exists to prove, so a green cross-path run on a journal case proves the store and nothing about the history; (2) it is worse than that today, because `fixture.root_sha256` is compared as a PRECONDITION ahead of everything else and a journal-bearing fixture's installed directory is named for a digest of the copy's own absolute path — so cross-path comparison of any journal case reports a HARNESS ERROR rather than running. Capture and compare at one absolute path, sequentially.

THREE OF THIS SLICE'S FIVE TESTS ARE SEQUENCES, NOT INVOCATIONS. One case is one invocation (porting/runners/README.md's case list: one argv, one process, one before/after pair, no vocabulary for a second process or an ordering). test_two_stores_share_one_history, test_shared_history_across_two_path_spellings and test_capping_keeps_only_recent_history_across_instances each require two or more Store instantiations against one file. (test_undo_survives_a_new_store_instance and test_redo_survives_a_new_store_instance were two more until the 2026-08-02 merge review moved them to `undo-redo-apply`; the same sentence applies to them there.) There is a real partial escape and it is how the corpus's two generated journal fixtures were built: a fixture may SHIP a journal/ that encodes the RESULT of a prior sequence, so a state reachable only by a sequence can be a case's INPUT. The sequence itself still cannot be a case.

The `org` guard's severity is the port-hostile part and one fixture proves it. `adversarial/journal-foreign-org` ships a literal index.json naming /home/someone-else/tasks/tasks.jsonl; a mismatch invalidates the ENTIRE history rather than skipping a state, because a 16-hex prefix collision, a restored backup or a copied home directory can put someone else's history at your key. A port that treated a mismatched org as 'ignore that field, the directory key already matched' would replay another store's states over this one's bytes. That fixture is also the corpus's only literal index.json — the other four are templates with {{ORG_PATH}} substituted at install time, which is the mechanism the same-path constraint above rests on.

The cap and the GC are two rules a port will merge and must not. `record` caps states at limit+1 and drops from the FRONT, adjusting the cursor by the same amount; `collect` then deletes any blob no surviving state references. GC is explicitly best-effort ('a leaked blob wastes a little disk, never breaks undo') and runs only when the state set may have SHRUNK — never on an undo/redo commit, 'so scanning the blob dir for it would be pure waste on the hot path'. The observation records blob count and sorted blob digests, so a port that GC'd on every commit is observably different on a redo case and a port that never GC'd is observably different on a capped one. Both are visible; neither is driven by any case today.

Content-addressed dedup is a CONSTRAINT ON THE PORT'S DESIGN, not a formatting detail, and delete-task's gap already records the evidence: `adversarial/journal-undo-redo-delete` and `journal-redo-pending-delete` hold eight states referencing five blobs, because a delete can land back on a blob an earlier capture already produced. A port that stores deltas rather than whole-file blobs cannot reproduce that index. Two further shapes those fixtures pin, also from delete-task's gap: org_sha is null at state 0 (the history predates the file) and undo restores `updated` stamps byte-exactly rather than refreshing them.

Journal.canonical's ENOENT branch has no fixture and cannot easily have one. When the org file does not exist yet (first-run capture), it resolves the containing DIRECTORY and appends the basename, so a /tmp → /private/tmp style symlink cannot shift the journal key between a capture and its undo. Reaching it needs a copy with no store file at all and a symlinked parent — `valid/empty-store` ships an empty store, not an absent one. It is one of the few places where getting it wrong produces a silently orphaned history rather than an error.

EVERY REMAINING TEST HERE PROVES THIS SLICE'S BEHAVIOR THROUGH `Store#undo!`, WHICH THIS SLICE DOES NOT PORT AND WHICH IS OWNED BY A DOWNSTREAM SLICE. `test_two_stores_share_one_history`, `test_shared_history_across_two_path_spellings`, `test_capping_keeps_only_recent_history_across_instances` and `test_journal_persists_only_between_matching_org` all call `undo!` — the first three as a round-trip assertion and the fourth only to assert `[:empty]`, i.e. the `org` guard refusing to load, which is genuinely this slice's. `undo-redo-apply` owns `undo!` and depends on this slice, so the edge that would make these refs reachable is the edge that would close a cycle; the 2026-08-02 merge review moved out the two tests whose SUBJECT was the round trip (`*_survives_a_new_store_instance`) and kept these four, whose subject is identity, sharing and capping. The instruction that follows is the one `manifest.md`'s `reach` section prescribes: characterization here must drive `Journal#record`, `#load` and `#intern` directly and assert the index and blob bytes, NOT run `undo!` and assert the store file. A capture that takes the easy path proves undo-redo-apply's behavior and calls it this slice's.

REDO-TAIL TRUNCATION IS DECLARED HERE AND PROVED ONLY DOWNSTREAM. The behavior sentence names it and `notes` says this slice ports `journal.rb:119-121`, but the only assertion in the repository is `test/test_store.rb#test_new_mutation_clears_redo`, which is `undo-redo-apply`'s — and `undo-redo-apply` DEPENDS ON this slice, so the oracle sits strictly downstream of the code it proves. There is no legal edge that fixes this and the clause is not deleted, because the truncation is real and a port that omits it corrupts history. What a port can get wrong while staying green at this slice's position: `#record` can append a new state WITHOUT dropping the states after the cursor, and every test claimed here still passes, because none of them redoes after a fresh mutation. The defect surfaces one slice later as a redo that replays a branch the user abandoned.

TWO CLAUSES OF THE BEHAVIOR SENTENCE ARE UNFALSIFIABLE AGAINST TODAY'S SUITE, CONFIRMED BY MUTATION (2026-08-02 merge review). (a) 'content-addressed DEDUPLICATED blobs': deleting the dedup early-return at `journal.rb:290` leaves the whole suite green — a port that re-writes an identical blob under its own digest every time is correct-looking and merely wasteful, and nothing detects it. (b) 'the blob GARBAGE COLLECTION': stubbing `Journal#collect` to a no-op also leaves the whole suite green. The only blob assertion in the repository is `test_blobs_are_garbage_collected_when_history_is_capped`'s `blobs <= UNDO_LIMIT + 2` — a bound of 52 against a real count of 3, which no plausible defect exceeds. So a port that never collects grows the state directory without limit and passes. (c) Separately, the directory key `sha256(realpath(org))[0,16]` is pinned by NO Ruby test: nothing asserts the digest, the truncation to 16 characters, or that `realpath` rather than the given path is digested. A port using a different hash, a different prefix length, or the unresolved path produces a journal directory Ruby cannot find and vice versa — invisible before cutover, and a silent loss of every user's undo history at it.

behavior: The journal's containment contract: every corrupt, missing, non-regular or hostile journal state degrades to `nothing to undo` and a fresh safe baseline — an out-of-range or non-integer cursor, a malformed state hash, a non-Hash index, a missing or tampered blob, a directory or symlink where a blob or the index belongs — while genuinely fatal errors still propagate and task bytes are never touched
oracle_gaps: THE DEGRADATION IS SILENT, WHICH MEANS THE OBSERVATION FOR 'HISTORY DAMAGED' AND 'HISTORY ABSENT' IS THE SAME. `adversarial/journal-missing-blob`'s README says so in as many words: 'the user is not told the history is damaged'. So stdout, stderr and exit status are identical between a store with no journal at all and a store whose journal was silently discarded, and the only distinguishing evidence is `journal.*` — the index bytes and blob digests before and after. Every case here must be a journal-bearing case whose BEFORE state is the damaged one, or it proves nothing: run the same argv against `valid/small-gtd` and the observation is indistinguishable.

EIGHT OF THE TEN DEGRADATIONS HAVE NO FIXTURE. The corpus ships one, `adversarial/journal-missing-blob`. The other nine states (out-of-range cursor, non-integer cursor, non-Hash index, malformed state hash, directory at the current blob, symlink at the current blob, directory at index.json, EACCES on a blob, EACCES on index.json) exist only inside the Ruby tests, which construct them by hand. Two of them cannot be shipped in git at all under the current protocol: an EACCES needs a mode git does not record for a path the runner creates, and the copy step (`cp -a`) plus the journal-install step create no non-regular entries of their own. Those two are recorded here as a permanent gap; the other seven ARE shippable and are requested below.

THE SYMLINK CASE IS A SECURITY PROPERTY AND THE ONE MOST LIKELY TO BE PORTED WRONG. Journal#regular_file? uses File.lstat(path).file? — an lstat, never a stat — so a symlink at a blob path is treated as absent, and `discard_nonregular` UNLINKS it rather than following it. A port using os.Stat (which follows) instead of os.Lstat passes every other test in this slice and, on the write side, would follow an attacker-placed symlink out of the journal directory and truncate the target. The blob path is derived from a digest and the journal lives under XDG_STATE_HOME, so this is a real local-attack surface. There is no observation field for 'the implementation called lstat'; the only evidence is that the symlink is gone and its target untouched, which requires a fixture that ships one.

'FATAL ERRORS STILL PROPAGATE' IS AN ABSENCE OF CONTAINMENT AND THE SCHEMA CANNOT ASSERT IT DIRECTLY. Journal#load, #plan and #record rescue SystemCallError, IOError, JSON::ParserError and CorruptBlob and nothing else; two tests pin the boundary by raising something outside that set and asserting it escapes. In an observation that is exit status plus stderr, and stderr for an escaping Ruby exception carries an absolute path, a line number and a Ruby-version-dependent backtrace rendering — bytes no port can match. This is the same hazard class campaign-10.md §4f found in `-p` with no words. Characterize the boundary as a translated unit test; do NOT build a case whose expected stderr is a Ruby backtrace.

The 'next record repairs history' half is what makes this a containment contract rather than a data-loss contract, and it is a SEQUENCE: three of these tests damage the journal, observe an empty undo, then perform a mutation and assert the history rebuilt from that mutation's before-state. One case is one invocation, so a case can observe the damaged read OR start from the damaged state and observe the rebuild, but not both in order. Two cases against one fixture is the workable shape and it is weaker than the test, because nothing ties them together.

Journal#record's own rescue is the widest containment in the file and has no test of its own: a SystemCallError or IOError anywhere in recording returns false, on the stated grounds that 'an unreadable or non-repairable journal must not roll back a task mutation that was already durably written'. That is the correct priority and it is also the branch where a port is most likely to be MORE careful than Ruby — failing the mutation because the history failed. Nothing in the suite or the corpus catches that inversion.

`undo-redo-apply` WAS ADDED AS A DEPENDENCY BY THE 2026-08-02 MERGE REVIEW AND THE EDGE IS REAL, NOT A `reach`-SILENCER. All ten tests here observe a damaged journal by calling `store.undo!` (three also `redo!`) and asserting `[:empty]` plus untouched task bytes. `undo!` is `undo-redo-apply`'s, and this slice previously declared only `journal-index-and-blobs`, which leaves the ordering impossible: there is no position in the graph at which any of these ten could go green. Adding the edge is sound because `undo-redo-apply` itself depends on `journal-index-and-blobs`, so the containment contract correctly sits downstream of both the store it contains and the apply path it contains. What the edge costs: the degradation outcome and the apply outcome are now proved at the same position, so a capture must distinguish 'undo returned empty because the journal was damaged' from 'undo returned empty because there was nothing to undo' — the two are byte-identical on stdout, which gap 0 above already records as this slice's central observation problem.

Two further states (EACCES on a blob, EACCES on index.json) are NOT requested: git records no mode for them and the copy protocol runs no commands, so they stay unit-test-proved. Every fixture also needs a second case driving a mutation from the damaged state, to observe the rebuild.

notes: Split out of journal-index-and-blobs deliberately: ten tests whose entire subject is containment against a hostile or damaged on-disk state, which is a threat-model review rather than a feature review. Folded into the happy path it becomes a seventeen-test slice whose reviewer reads the interesting two. Platforms exclude windows because three of the states (a symlink at a blob, a directory where a file belongs with POSIX rmdir semantics, an EACCES on a path readable by its owner) do not reproduce there without a different construction; the containment RULE is platform-independent and must hold, the fixtures are not.

behavior: Applying an undo or redo: the plan (label from the higher-indexed state, `expect` and `target` snapshots, a commit that strips all coalescing metadata), the precondition that refuses when live bytes do not match `expect`, restoring both files with archive-first ordering when a sweep is replayed, the restore-validity gate, the `repair` exemption from that gate, the empty and unsupported-schema outcomes, and a new mutation dropping the redo tail
oracle_gaps: THE `repair` FLAG IS THE MOST IMPORTANT FIELD IN THIS SLICE AND NO FIXTURE CARRIES IT. All five shipped journal fixtures were read: none of their indexes contains `repair`, `coalesce_key` or `coalesce_scope`, even though porting/runners/README.md says the runner parses all three into the observation. The rule is that a restored live file is gated on Check passing — EXCEPT when the step is marked repair, because its before-state is the malformed record the user deliberately asked to fix, so undo must faithfully restore invalid bytes rather than refuse. store-repair (campaign 4, td-d6ed92/td-2addce) sets the same flag for `tasks repair`; this slice now SHARE-CLAIMS its test_repair.rb#test_undo_restores_the_malformed_bytes, which is legal and reachable because store-repair is upstream, and is the only local oracle the exemption has. The TARGETED-repair path through a field patch is driven by test_cli_schedule_repair_is_one_journal_entry_undone_to_invalid_bytes, which the 2026-08-02 merge review moved DOWNSTREAM to `cli-date-verbs`: it runs `tasks schedule`, a verb this slice does not port, so it could never pass here, and the edge that would have fixed that closes a cycle against the journal edge campaign 5 owes back. The consequence to carry: the gate's targeted-repair branch is proved only at a downstream position, so a defect in it surfaces as a `cli-date-verbs` failure. A port that gates unconditionally leaves the user unable to undo the repair they just asked for; a port that never gates lets an ordinary undo restore a state failing today's invariants. Both pass every existing case.

THE ARCHIVE-FIRST RESTORE ORDERING IS A CORRECTNESS RULE WITH ONE INPUT SHAPE AND NO FIXTURE. Store#restore_archive_first? installs the destination copy before removing the source copy — archive first for live→archive (redo of a sweep), live first for archive→live (undo of one) — so an interruption leaves retry-safe duplicates and never a lost task. Reaching it needs a journal state pair whose org and archive BOTH change and whose ids move between them, i.e. a journal recording an archive sweep. `valid/archive-pair` has the two files and no journal; the five journal fixtures have no sweep. archive-sweep's own gap reserved test_undo_archive_sweep_restores_both_files for campaign 6, and the 2026-08-02 merge review executed that reservation: archive-sweep is now a depends_on and the test is share-claimed here. That gave the clause an ORACLE, not a CASE — the sweep-bearing journal fixture this gap asks for is still owed, and until it exists the ordering is proved by a translated unit test rather than by conformance.

test_undo_refuses_after_external_edit is the one behavior here the corpus DOES drive well, stated so the caveats above are not read as 'nothing works'. `adversarial/journal-cursor-behind-store` ships a seven-mutation history at the tip beside a store edited out of band, which is exactly the `snapshot != step[:expect]` branch; the outcome is a [:conflict, label] refusal leaving the foreign edit intact. It is the cleanest single conformance case in campaign 6.

behavior: Recovering when the undo or redo itself fails: a cursor commit that fails after installing the new index, an org or archive restore that fails, the exactly-once cursor rollback retry and the twice-attempted file rollback, keeping the archive's absence or its copy rather than a split state, and rolling files back before letting a fatal exception propagate
oracle_gaps: NOT ONE OF THESE NINE TESTS CAN BE A CONFORMANCE CASE, AND THE REASON IS STRUCTURAL RATHER THAN A CORPUS GAP. Every one injects a failure at a specific point INSIDE one operation, by stubbing Tasks::Atomic.write to raise for one particular path (test/test_journal.rb's with_atomic_write_denied helper). porting/runners/README.md offers exactly one crash point from outside the process — `copy_root_mode`, which makes the FIRST write fail — and explicitly rejected a fault-injection hook in the implementation for Phase 1 as 'a test seam every port would have to reimplement identically before it could be compared, and a seam whose own fidelity nothing checks'. The playbook's step 7 wants crash points around lock, write, flush, validation, rename AND journal append; one is available and it is at the wrong point for all nine. This slice is proved by translated unit tests, in the same honest-but-not-differential position agent-diff-report occupies in campaign 10.

THE PROPERTY UNDER TEST IS THE ABSENCE OF A SPLIT STATE, AND `files.rolled_back` CANNOT REPORT IT. That field is read from the implementation's own --json error envelope and is null when nothing was reported; these failures surface as a [:conflict, label] return, not as a rollback envelope, so on a hypothetical case the field would be null and the deltas empty — indistinguishable from 'nothing happened'. What must be asserted is a CONJUNCTION across four things (org bytes, archive presence, archive bytes, journal cursor) all simultaneously at their original values, which the schema can express only as 'no deltas', and 'no deltas' is exactly what a port that never attempted the undo also produces.

RETRY COUNTS ARE BEHAVIOR HERE AND ARE INVISIBLE EVERYWHERE. rollback_history_cursor tries the rollback lambda TWICE and rollback_history_files tries restore TWICE, comparing snapshots exactly (including nil absence) after each. test_transient_rollback_write_failure_retries_without_split_state and test_cursor_rollback_retries_when_commit_failed_after_installing_index distinguish a port that retries from one that gives up on the first failure — and a port that retries FOREVER, or once more, is indistinguishable from the correct one in every observation. The counts survive only as translated unit tests with an injected counting writer.

The rollback lambda is idempotent by an explicit guard no test names directly: it re-loads the index and re-persists the original cursor ONLY IF the current index differs from the captured one ('Atomic.write failures ordinarily leave the old index untouched. If a wrapper/filesystem reports failure after installing the new index, restore the captured cursor and state metadata exactly once'). A port that unconditionally rewrote would clobber a concurrent writer's index in the one case where the failure was spurious. Nothing catches it.

Five of these nine tests drive Store#archive_swept! to build a state pair where the archive appears or disappears, which is why archive-sweep (campaign 7) is a real dependency edge rather than an explained reach — the archive-absent/archive-present asymmetry IS the behavior, and archive_swept! is the only verb in the store that produces it. archive-sweep's own oracle_gaps already reserves test_undo_archive_sweep_restores_both_files for campaign 6; that sentence should name undo-redo-apply for the restore and this slice for the ordering guarantee under failure.

`Exception` is rescued, not just StandardError, and the ordering is contract: a fatal error rolls the FILES back first and only then re-raises, so an Interrupt during a cursor commit still leaves a consistent store. Re-raising an escaping error produces stderr bytes carrying a path, a line number and a Ruby-version-dependent rendering — uncapturable as a baseline, the same hazard campaign-10.md §4f recorded for `-p`. Characterize the FILE STATE after the fatal error, never the stderr.

behavior: Collapsing an editor session into one undo step: the six conjuncts that let a keyed mutation replace the tip in place (matching key, matching scope, cursor at tip, cursor positive, previous state's blobs verify, recorded tip matches the caller's before-state), the persisted `coalesce_scope` that stops an unrelated process extending a segment, the repair flag surviving an in-place replacement, and the pinned scope that makes journal bytes reproducible
oracle_gaps: NO FIXTURE IN THE CORPUS CARRIES A `coalesce_key` OR A `coalesce_scope`. All five shipped journal indexes were read and none contains either field, although porting/runners/README.md states the runner parses both into the observation. This is the same failure one level up that campaign-10.md §4b found against llm-provider-registry: a fixture set that reads as adequate to whoever builds it, against which a port that DROPPED COALESCING ENTIRELY — recording every keyed patch as its own state — emits a byte-identical observation on every existing case, because no existing case supplies a key. The corpus cannot currently falsify the central behavior of this slice.

TWELVE OF SEVENTEEN TESTS REQUIRE A SECOND STORE INSTANCE OR AN INTERVENING WRITE, AND ONE CASE IS ONE INVOCATION. Every 'break' test is a sequence by construction: an intervening CLI mutation, an external absolute write, an undo/redo between two keyed patches, a history branch, a fresh Store instance, foreign org bytes, foreign archive bytes. porting/runners/README.md's case list has one argv, one process and one before/after pair, with no vocabulary for a second invocation against the same copy or an ordering between two. test_two_pinned_runs_produce_identical_stores_and_journals is two runs by definition. The escape used elsewhere in this campaign — ship a journal encoding the result of a prior sequence — gives a case the STARTING tip; it cannot supply the second patch that must or must not coalesce onto it, so each break test becomes at best two loosely coupled cases.

THE RULE IS SIX CONJUNCTS AND A PORT THAT IMPLEMENTS FIVE PASSES MOST OF THE SUITE. Journal#record coalesces only when the key is a String AND the recorded tip matches the caller's before-state AND the cursor is at the last state AND the cursor is positive AND the tip's coalesce_key equals the key AND the tip's coalesce_scope equals this Journal's scope AND the PREVIOUS state's blobs still verify. Each break test targets one conjunct, which is exactly why they are one slice: split three ways, each piece proves one `&&` and nothing proves the conjunction. The cursor-positive clause is the one with no independent test — it prevents coalescing onto the baseline state, which has no label to inherit.

THE DEFAULT SCOPE IS `SecureRandom.hex(16)` AND IS PERSISTED INTO JOURNAL BYTES, so an unpinned run's index.json differs from itself run twice. porting/specs/determinism.md pins it with TASKS_PIN_COALESCE_SCOPE and the runner sets it to `pinned-scope`. But test_store_factory_defaults_to_a_random_coalesce_scope asserts the UNPINNED behavior — that two factories mint different scopes — which is precisely what the pin removes, so that one test can never be a conformance case and must stay a translated unit test. The pin's necessity is the finding: without it two correct implementations disagree on journal bytes for reasons neither owns.

THE REPAIR FLAG SURVIVING AN IN-PLACE REPLACEMENT IS A ONE-LINE RULE WITH ONE TEST AND A CATASTROPHIC FAILURE MODE. Journal#record copies `state[:repair] = true if states[cursor][:repair]` when coalescing, because the replaced step's BEFORE-state is still the malformed bytes and the exemption must survive the overwrite — otherwise undoing the coalesced step hits the restore-validity gate and REFUSES to restore the user's original bytes. store-repair (campaign 4) sets the same flag from `tasks repair`; this slice owns its survival across coalescing, and test_coalescing_onto_a_repair_step_keeps_the_undo_exemption is its only oracle anywhere. No fixture carries a `repair` flag either.

The Application half is a different mechanism with the same name and must not be merged into the Journal half. StoreFactory builds a FRESH Store per call (test_every_application_call_gets_a_fresh_store_instance) and injects one shared coalesce_scope for the Application's lifetime, which is the only reason keyed patches across those fresh stores collapse into one undo step. A port that made Application hold one Store would pass test_keyed_patches_across_fresh_stores_coalesce_into_one_undo_step for the wrong reason and lose the per-operation isolation the facade exists for. Both tests are claimed here because neither is meaningful alone.

lib/tasks/determinism.rb is named in source_paths and is named by NO other record in the manifest. It sits in several closures transitively, so drift has watched it; naming it makes a change to the coalesce-scope pin attributable. This slice ports only that pin's seam — the clock, id, device, hostname and winsize pins belong to update-stamp, id-minting, config-resolution and campaign 12 respectively — and says so here rather than letting the closure imply otherwise, following campaign-10.md §6's rule for a shared file.

oracle_gaps: THE BEHAVIOR IS 'MUTATE IN PROCESS A, UNDO IN PROCESS B', AND ONE CASE IS ONE INVOCATION. All four tests spawn at least two real `tasks` processes against one org file and one XDG_STATE_HOME; porting/runners/README.md's case list has one argv and one process. The workable substitute is the whole reason the corpus's journal fixtures exist: process A's effect is SHIPPED as the fixture's journal/, and the case is process B. That is a good substitute for the undo itself and a poor one for the claim these tests actually make — that a history written by one process is legible to another — because the fixture's journal was written by the Ruby, so a case only proves the port can READ Ruby's history, never that the port's own writes are readable by a second instance of the port. behavior: The published OpenAPI 3.1 document as a contract artifact: every embedded request and response example validates against its own schemas, nullable unions and local $refs resolve, `additionalProperties: false` rejects unknown body fields, TaskPlacement admits only parent_id/before_id, the PATCH description freezes the revision-scope wording, no operation carries a duplicate response key, and every documented 409 carries only domain conflict codes
oracle_gaps: METHOD, DECIDED AND NOT A GAP TO CLOSE LATER: THIS SLICE IS PROVED BY TRANSLATED UNIT TESTS, NOT BY DIFFERENTIAL CONFORMANCE. `surface: "http"` is reserved in porting/specs/observations.schema.json and unimplemented in the runner, whose known-gaps list says flatly "`http` is always empty and `surface` is always `cli`"; the only HTTP field anywhere in the schema is `revisions.http_etag` — no status code, no request or response headers, no response body distinct from process stdout, no method, no path — and the eleven-step copy-per-case protocol (copy, probe, invoke ONE argv, probe, emit) has no place for a long-lived server that must be started, driven N times and stopped. Building an HTTP surface into the conformance harness would be a large investment to prove one campaign, and Marcus's call (2026-08-01) is that it is not worth its cost: this is a personal task manager and the API is a secondary surface behind the CLI and the TUI. The Go port therefore reimplements test/api/* against the Go server and THOSE tests are this slice's evidence, in the same shape as `agent-request-queue`. THE CONSEQUENCE, stated so that nobody later reads the empty `fixtures` as an oversight: a fully green conformance run proves NOTHING about this slice, because no case in the corpus touches the HTTP surface at all. `fixtures_todo` is deliberately null — do not write one asking for an HTTP surface.

This slice is the one place in campaign 9 where the translated-unit-test method is not a compromise: the subject is a YAML document, not a running server, and every assertion is a pure function of that document's bytes. What DOES change in the port is the validator. The Ruby oracle runs `openapi_first`, a third-party gem; a Go port will run a different OpenAPI 3.1 library with different strictness. `test_unknown_query_fields_require_an_explicit_adapter_guard` is the standing proof that library strictness is not the contract — it asserts, with the reason in the assertion message, that openapi_first accepts an undocumented query parameter and therefore that the ADAPTER must compare raw and documented query keys itself. A Go library that happens to reject it would make that test vacuously pass while the adapter guard rots. Port the assertion as a statement about the adapter, not about the library.

`test_409_contracts_have_unique_keys_and_carry_only_domain_conflicts` walks `/history/undo`, `/history/redo` and `/archive-sweeps` — three operations the server does not route (see `api-unrouted-endpoints`). Their 409 documentation is therefore contract-only, asserted here, and implemented nowhere. That is intentional, and it is exactly why this slice is separate from every slice that has a route behind it.

The duplicate-response-key check is implemented by re-reading the YAML file LINE BY LINE with four regexes, not by parsing it, because a YAML parser silently keeps the last of two duplicate keys and the defect it is guarding against is invisible after parsing. A port that reimplements this over a parsed document proves nothing. The Go equivalent must also read the raw bytes.

Nothing in this suite, `drift`, or the conformance harness compares the document to the SERVER. Contract/implementation agreement is asserted only by the `assert_contract_response` / `assert_contract_exchange` helpers inside the other campaign 9 test files, which validate live responses against this document — so a divergence between the two is caught by those slices' tests and never by this one.

notes: `docs/api/openapi.yaml` is the only source path in this campaign that is neither under lib/ nor bin/, so it sits in no drift closure today and no record watches it. Naming it here puts a 3600-line published contract under `drift` for the first time. The document is also larger than the server: it documents seven paths the server does not route, and `test_locked_toolchain_loads_the_openapi_31_contract` asserts only `routes.count >= 10`, so nothing here notices a path being added to the document alone. NO FIXTURE IS WIRED, AND THE REASON IS NARROWER THAN THIS RECORD USED TO CLAIM. The sentence the 2026-08-02 merge review replaced here said an HTTP request is something "the case list cannot express and the observation schema cannot record". Both halves are false. `porting/runners/README.md` gives every case a `surface` field whose `"http"` value is reserved for the phase that ports the adapter, and `porting/specs/observations.schema.json` carries a top-level `http` array of request/response items added expressly so that "a Phase-1 harness that captures HTTP oracle output has somewhere honest to put it". THREE TAG PROJECTIONS EXIST AND THIS IS THE STRICTEST. `task-view-projection`'s gap already names the trio and pins it on `porting/fixtures/valid/deferred-tags`: record de000003 projects as ["defer", "@computer", "research"] under TaskView and as ["research"] under `Representation.task`. Note that the same view's `contexts` field carries the @-prefixed values, so nothing is lost — but a port that reuses TaskView#tags here leaks `defer` and every @context into the HTTP `tags` array, and `test_task_representation_and_source_exact_lookup` catches it only because the fixture task carries exactly one ordinary tag beside a context. That fixture pins the divergence for the CLI side; there is no HTTP case that can read it.

The delegation object is passed through UNTOUCHED — `delegation: view.delegation` with no re-serialization — so the HTTP resource, `tasks show --json` and the record on disk are one set of bytes in one key order. `test_task_resource_carries_the_stored_delegation_verbatim` asserts `delegation.keys == %w[kind mode status assignee at work_ref]` positionally and asserts a human hand-off omits `mode` entirely. A Go port that models the delegation as a struct with `omitempty` gets the omission right and the ORDER wrong the moment the struct field order is edited; a port that models it as a map gets neither. The stored key order is `delegation-record-shape`'s KEY_ORDER and this slice must consume it, not restate it.

`archived: view.source == :archive` and `source: view.source.to_s` are two encodings of the same fact in one resource, and `project: view.project || view.section_title` silently falls back. `available=false` is refused unless `scope=open`, and `available=true` is accepted with ANY scope — including archived, where availability is meaningless. The refusal is asserted; the asymmetry is not.

THIS SLICE HAS TWO TESTS AND ITS BEHAVIOR IS ASSERTED IN ABOUT FORTY PLACES, which is the opposite of the usual problem and needs saying. Almost every test in test/api/ carries an incidental `assert_equal quote(payload.dig("data","revision")), response["etag"]` or feeds one response's ETag into the next request's If-Match; those assertions belong to the slices that own those routes. The two tests claimed here are the only ones whose SUBJECT is the protocol: the 428/422/412 ladder and the shape of the 412 body. A port that broke ETag quoting would fail dozens of tests across every slice; a port that dropped `details.current` from the 412 would fail only these two.

412 vs 409 IS A DESIGNED DISTINCTION AND HALF OF IT IS OWNED ELSEWHERE. The Ruby writes the rule out in a comment block: 412 stale_revision means the task moved on since the client read it (refetch and decide again); 409 claim_conflict means the client's view was current and the delegation is simply held by someone else (pick another task, or revoke). `test_every_action_requires_a_well_formed_if_match` proves the 412 half over all five delegation routes; `test_lost_claim_race_is_409_while_a_stale_precondition_is_412` (owned by `api-delegation-actions`) proves both halves against one another. Neither slice can prove the distinction alone.

THE `own` COMPONENT'S SCOPE IS THE HARDEST THING HERE AND IT IS CAMPAIGN 6's. A task's revision deliberately does NOT change when only an ancestor moves — `test_parent_null_unnests_and_tree_counts_are_derived` (owned by `api-task-write-lifecycle`) asserts a grandchild's ETag is byte-identical after its parent is moved by a separate Store process — and the PATCH contract's description freezes the wording (`api-openapi-contract` asserts the strings "content-only `own` component" and "`own` digest excludes structural location" are present). This slice ports the transport of that component and NOT its computation. A dependency edge on campaign 6's revision slice is owed and cannot be written yet: campaigns 5, 6 and 12 are being seeded in parallel and their ids do not exist in porting/manifest.jsonl at the time this record was written. Add it when they merge.

`if_match!` accepts exactly one shape: `/\A"([^"\\]+)"\z/`. That means no weak validators (`W/"..."`), no `*`, no comma-separated list, and no unquoted token — all four of which are legal If-Match syntax in RFC 9110 and all four of which a Go HTTP library may hand through or normalize. Only "not-an-etag" is tested. A port using a standards-compliant If-Match parser will accept `*` and change a 422 into a successful unconditional write, which is the single most dangerous divergence available in this campaign.

THIS SLICE'S ORACLE REACHES DOWNSTREAM AND `reach` FLAGS IT. `test_preconditions_stale_current_and_delete_cascade_conflict` manufactures the stale condition by opening a second `Tasks::Store` and driving `apply_changeset!` directly — a verb `changeset-apply-basic` owns and which is not upstream of this slice. That is correct and no dependency edge is added: a stale precondition needs SOME competing writer, not that particular one, and the same test's second half drives a cascading DELETE for the 409. It is the same shape `agent-diff-report` recorded for its `capture` drive, and this sentence is what makes the reach explained rather than silently tolerated.

The 412 body's `details.current` is populated ONLY when the current task can be re-read (`current&.ok?`); when it cannot, the 412 goes out with empty details and NO ETag header, and nothing tests that path. A client written against the documented shape will find `details.current` missing exactly when the store has just become unreadable.

PATCH and DELETE require If-Match; the project routes deliberately do NOT (`test_projects.rb#test_rename_requires_no_if_match`, owned by `api-project-rename-and-complete`), because the domain exposes no per-section revision. That parity difference is documented in the OpenAPI contract and is the one place where a mutating route in this API is unconditioned.

THE HOST-CONTEXT BEHAVIOR THIS SLICE PROVES IS UNREACHABLE THROUGH THE REAL SERVER. `test_create_adds_configured_host_context_and_supports_explicit_opt_out` builds the app directly with `Tasks::Config.for_dir(@dir)` and a hand-set `paths.host_context`. This is a product bug, not a manifest bug; it is recorded here and on `api-server-entrypoint` and should be filed for Marcus. The port must reproduce the omission or Marcus must decide to fix it — a Go port that "helpfully" threads host_context through the entrypoint is landing a behavior change under cover of a port.

No dependency edge is written for it — this slice needs SOME journal, not a particular one — following the precedent `agent-diff-report` set for its `capture` drive.

THE UNNEST-UNDER-LOCK RULE IS THE SUBTLEST BEHAVIOR IN THE SLICE. `normalize_patch_changes` maps `parent_id: null` to `TaskChangeset::UNNEST` rather than to a section id the adapter looked up, and the Ruby says why in a comment: Store resolves nil to the enclosing section under the mutation lock, so a concurrent ancestor move cannot reuse a stale section observed by a separate adapter read. `test_parent_null_unnests_and_tree_counts_are_derived` proves it by moving an ancestor through a second Store instance between the client's read and its unnest, and asserting the unnest lands in the NEW section. A port that resolves the section in the adapter passes every other test in this campaign and loses a task into the wrong section under exactly the interleaving the API exists to support.

The `:cycle`/`:too_deep` arms are reached only from `api-ordered-placement`, `:unsupported_schema` only from `api-read-model-and-store-revision`, and the terminal `else` (503 unavailable) by nothing. PLACEMENT IS THE DRAG-AND-DROP CONTRACT AND THE WHOLE DESIGN IS ABOUT WHAT DOES *NOT* INVALIDATE A FETCH. The client fetches a collection once, the user drags, and the PATCH must succeed even though every sibling's location fingerprint churned in between — because the `own` component the ETag carries excludes structural location. `test_ordered_placement_accepts_before_null_and_omitted_anchors_from_one_fetch` reuses ONE pre-drag ETag for three successive placements after two reorders and asserts all three succeed. `test_placement_stales_on_own_edit_while_legacy_parent_move_still_guards_location` is its mirror: a CLI edit to the moving task's own CONTENT does stale it (412), and the legacy `parent_id` form keeps its separate location comparison and stales where the placement form would not. A port that compares a whole-record digest passes nothing here; a port that compares nothing passes everything here and loses updates. The component split itself is campaign 6's; this slice proves the transport consequences.

409 claim_conflict IS A DISTINCT CODE FROM 409 conflict AND FROM 412 stale_revision, AND THE THREE-WAY DISTINCTION IS THE SLICE. `delegation_failure!` intercepts `:conflict` before the shared mapper so that a lost race carries {id, action, holder, at} — the holder's worker id and the timestamp of the transition that beat this request — while every other refusal falls through to `mutation_failure!` with `semantic_invalid: true`. `test_lost_claim_race_is_409_while_a_stale_precondition_is_412` drives both from the same starting ETag and asserts the two apart, including that a holder re-claiming its own task is still 409. `holder` is null in the one case where a worker acts on a marker nobody holds, and that case is asserted by nothing.

THE ROUTE IS DISPATCHED BY `send(:"#{verb}_task_action", ...)` FROM A REGEX CAPTURE. The regex admits exactly four literal verbs so the dispatch cannot name anything else, and the Ruby comment says so — but this is dynamic dispatch on user-controlled path input, and a Go port has no equivalent idiom and should not invent one. Translate it as an explicit four-way switch; the property to preserve is that no fifth verb is reachable, which `test_unrouted_delegation_verbs_and_media_types_are_refused` (owned by `api-routing-and-service-metadata`) proves for three shapes.

`delegation_response` RE-READS ONLY ON THE IDEMPOTENT PATH. Application already re-reads the task from the snapshot its own write produced, so the response cannot show a neighbouring writer's later state and its ETag is the revision THIS request created. There is no If-Match to close the window because the domain exposes no section revision. No test races it, the observation schema cannot express it, and campaign 6's locking slices are about a different boundary (the shared inventory §3e: which side of `Store#with_lock` the test observes from). DEFERRED WORK BLOCKS AND THAT IS THE NON-OBVIOUS HALF. `held_count` is summed with `open_count`, so a project whose only remaining task is deferred still refuses without force — parity with complete's cascade, which closes deferred tasks too. `test_archive_refuses_a_deferred_only_project_then_force_sweeps` is the only proof and it needs its own fixture (DEFERRED_ONLY_FIXTURE, built inline in the test file). A port that used only `open_count` passes five of these seven tests.

`test_archive_force_never_sweeps_an_undecided_proposal` is a DOMAIN guarantee asserted from the adapter: force is force for open work and is NOT force for an undecided proposal, which survives the sweep. That rule belongs to `archive-project`/`archive-sweep`; this slice proves the HTTP path does not have its own back door around it. If the domain rule changed, this test would fail here and give no hint that the cause was elsewhere.

The response body is assembled by hand — `{id, archived, moved_ids}` where `archived` falls back from `result.summary[:archived]` to `result.touched_ids.length` when the summary is absent. The fallback is reached by nothing and the two values are not guaranteed equal: `touched_ids` is every record the mutation touched, `summary[:archived]` is what the sweep counted. A port that keeps only one of them will be right most of the time.

The ETag comes from a SEPARATE `read_status_result` taken after the sweep — a fourth store read in one request, after the pre-read, the force pre-check read and the write. Same unguarded window as `api-project-rename-and-complete`'s, one read wider.

This is the one route in the API that moves records BETWEEN FILES, so its correctness depends on the archive file as much as the live one, and the global store revision digests both (`api-read-model-and-store-revision`). `test_live_and_archive_external_changes_advance_refresh_token_and_reads_are_fresh` (owned by `api-cross-process-freshness`) is the only test in the campaign that proves the archive half of that digest participates at all.

THE ENTRYPOINT DROPS host_context AND NO TEST NOTICES. `bin/tasks-api` serializes nine keys into TASKS_API_RESOLVED_CONFIG — org, archive, urgent_days, max_depth, timezone, time_format, links, link_systems, port — and `config.ru` rebuilds `Config::Paths` from exactly those nine. `host_context` is not among them and defaults to nil, so a user with `host_context.<hostname>` configured gets the context applied by `tasks capture` and NOT by POST /api/v1/tasks through the real server. THE TWO-PROCESS HAND-OFF HAS NO GO ANALOGUE AND MUST NOT BE TRANSLATED LITERALLY. The Ruby resolves config, stuffs JSON into an environment variable, and `exec`s `bundle exec puma config.ru`, which re-reads that variable in a fresh process. That shape exists because Rack config files are loaded by the server, not by the app. A Go server is one process with an HTTP handler; the behavior to preserve is that configuration is resolved ONCE, before listening, and that a server started any other way refuses to run (config.ru's `abort "tasks-api must be started through bin/tasks-api"`). The environment variable itself is an implementation detail of the Ruby stack.

`test_real_entrypoint_starts_and_stops_cleanly` asserts a SIGINT exit is `status.success?`. Nothing asserts SIGTERM, nothing asserts in-flight requests are drained, and nothing asserts the listening socket is released. `teardown` sends TERM and escalates to KILL after five seconds without asserting which one worked, so a server that ignores TERM entirely passes the whole suite — the same escalation-ladder blindness `agent-harness-protocol`'s gaps record for the harness child.

THE THREE ABORT PATHS ARE PROVED BY NOTHING: a non-loopback `--bind`, a port outside 1..65535, and the missing-dependency abort are each one line in `bin/tasks-api` with no test at all. The loopback restriction is the security posture of the entire product — this server has no authentication and its only defence is that it cannot be reached from another host — and it is enforced by a single string comparison that no test exercises. Any translated-unit-test suite for this slice must add coverage the Ruby never had; that is the one place in this campaign where the port should NOT stop at parity of proof.

`test_real_puma_boots_the_rack_lint_config` boots puma against `test/api/fixtures/toolchain.ru`, a two-line Rack::Lint-wrapped lambda, and asserts one 200. What it proves is that the locked server toolchain can serve a Rack-compliant app at all — a dependency smoke test, not a behavior of this product. In Go it becomes a smoke test of net/http and should be kept as one rather than deleted, because its real function is to fail loudly when the server stack is broken independently of the application.

The two startup lines printed before the exec (`tasks-api listening on http://127.0.0.1:<port>` and `tasks source: <path>; archive source: <path>`) are observable stdout that names ABSOLUTE PATHS. Nothing asserts them, and they are the one place in this campaign where the server deliberately prints a store path — the opposite of the no-path-leak rule every HTTP response obeys.

THIS IS THE SLICE THE CONFORMANCE PROTOCOL IS FURTHEST FROM EXPRESSING, and the reason is not the HTTP surface. `porting/runners/README.md`'s case list is one fixture, one argv, one process, one before/after pair; there is no vocabulary for a second process, a second invocation against the same copy, an interleaving, or an ordering between them. These four tests spawn a server, spawn between two and six `bin/tasks` subprocesses, and interleave them with `Queue`-synchronized threads. Even a fully implemented `surface: "http"` would not make them expressible. Campaign 6 hits the identical wall from the other side (`test_journal.rb#test_concurrent_writers_do_not_lose_updates`, the coalescing-break tests, `test_cli_delete_is_undoable_across_processes`); the shared inventory §3e records that these are the SAME invariant observed through two adapters and that the port needs both proofs.

THE CROSS-ADAPTER BYTE-EQUALITY ASSERTION IS THE STRONGEST IN THE PRODUCT AND IT IS ALSO THE MOST FRAGILE. `test_ordered_placements_survive_cli_churn_and_match_stable_id_cli_bytes` performs two placements over HTTP against one store and the equivalent two `tasks move` commands against a byte-identical copy in another directory, then compares the two files after stripping `updated` and `line` from only the two moved records. Everything else — key order, id minting, section membership, the untouched records' `updated` stamps — must match byte for byte across two adapters and two processes. A port whose HTTP path and CLI path build the same changeset through different code will fail here and nowhere else. The normalization is narrow ON PURPOSE and a port must not widen it to make a failure go away; that is the "never bless Go output" rule applied to a comparison rather than to an expectation.

THE RACE IS 8 ROUNDS AND ASSERTS ONLY THAT NOTHING WAS LOST. `test_cli_capture_racing_api_creates_preserves_every_successful_write` synchronizes two threads on a pair of Queues, fires a POST and a `tasks capture` simultaneously, and afterwards asserts every title is present and `Check` passes. It does not assert an ORDER, does not assert either writer retried, and does not assert the lock was contended at all — on a fast machine the two may simply not overlap. So a green run is evidence of no corruption and NOT evidence that mutual exclusion held. determinism.md's note that the lock file stays visible in `files.deltas` is the nearest the harness gets, and it is not available here.

UNDO ACROSS PROCESSES IS PROVED TWICE AND BOTH TIMES BY BYTES. `test_api_mutation_is_undone_by_fresh_cli_process_to_exact_bytes_and_resource` asserts the file returns to its exact prior bytes AND that the re-read HTTP resource equals the pre-mutation resource object — a stronger pair than either alone, because byte equality could coexist with a stale server-side cache and resource equality could coexist with a rewritten file. The journal that makes this work is campaign 6's and unseeded; a dependency edge is owed and cannot be written yet.

The CLI half of every one of these tests shells out to `bin/tasks` with `RbConfig.ruby`, so the ORACLE for this slice is the CLI's behavior in six campaigns' worth of slices. `reach` cannot see any of it: VERB_OWNERS maps store mutation verbs, and these oracles reach downstream through both an HTTP route and a CLI verb. No dependency edges are written for the CLI verbs — this slice needs a working CLI, not a particular slice — following `agent-diff-report`'s precedent.

`without_update_stamps` strips `updated` because wall-clock stamps differ between two runs; `TASKS_PIN_NOW` would remove the need, and the black-box suite does not use it. A Go port that pins the clock in these tests would be strengthening the assertion, which is an improvement to raise rather than to land silently.

NO CACHE IS THE BEHAVIOR, AND IT IS PROVED ONLY BY ITS ABSENCE. Every API read takes a fresh checked snapshot through a fresh Store (`Application#checked_query` calls `store_factory.call` each time), so a server that has been running for hours sees a `vim` edit to tasks.jsonl on the very next request. `test_live_and_archive_external_changes_advance_refresh_token_and_reads_are_fresh` proves it for both files by writing them from outside and asserting the /meta revision changed and the new content is readable. THE OBVIOUS OPTIMIZATION — cache the snapshot, invalidate on mtime — breaks this and only this test, and breaks it in a way that looks like flakiness (a filesystem with coarse mtime granularity would make it intermittent). A Go port must treat "re-read every request" as the contract, not as a naive implementation to improve.

THE ARCHIVE FILE PARTICIPATES IN THE REVISION AND THIS IS THE ONLY TEST THAT SAYS SO. `store_revision_for_contents` digests live and archive bytes together; a port that digests only the live file passes every other test in the campaign, because nothing else in test/api/ writes the archive from outside. `api-read-model-and-store-revision` owns the digest, this slice owns the proof.

THE THREE-WAY PLACEMENT DISCRIMINATION IS RE-PROVED HERE ACROSS PROCESSES ON PURPOSE. `api-ordered-placement` proves 412/404/409 against a second `Store` object in the same process; `test_placement_distinguishes_stale_own_edit_missing_anchor_and_moved_anchor` proves the same three against real `bin/tasks` subprocesses (retitle, delete, move) while a real server holds no state between them. The duplication is the point — the in-process version could pass with a shared object graph that a second process would not have. Both are needed and neither is redundant.

THE PATH-LEAK CHECK EXTENDS TO THE SERVER LOG AND IS THE ONLY PLACE IT DOES. `test_invalid_external_edit_refuses_reads_and_mutations_without_overwrite_or_path_leak` asserts `refute_includes server_log, @dir` — the puma stdout/stderr captured from the spawned process, which includes anything the Rack stack or the runtime printed, not just this product's JSON log lines. A Go port that lets net/http log a panic, or that writes a stack trace on a recovered handler, fails here and passes every unit test. It is also a NEGATIVE assertion (see `api-transport-envelope`'s third gap) and passes vacuously if the server writes nothing at all.

`assert_equal invalid, File.binread(@org)` is the assertion that the refused mutation did not overwrite the corrupted file — proving the write was refused BEFORE the write, which is `ensure_store_ready!`. It is the only end-to-end proof of that ordering in the campaign; `test_an_unsupported_schema_version_is_refused_on_read_and_on_write` proves the same shape for a schema version in-process.

The same one-case-one-invocation wall as `api-cross-process-writes` applies here in full and is not repeated: no case list can express a spawned server, an external file edit, and a subsequent request against the same copy.
